January 19, 1988

1 pointed out yesterday that the board which will be directing the activities of the agency is only there to assist the Minister. The Minister and the Deputy Minister are here in Ottawa. There is no decentralization. This is a continuation of the concept that everything that will happen in Atlantic Canada will be determined here in Ottawa. In fact, the Deputy Minister of this agency, Mr. McPhail, said that the agency will not be concerned with macroeconomic programs in Atlantic Canada. That is, in fact, contradicted by Mr. Deneen, who said that they are concerned about programs for Atlantic Canada in a regional perspective. Indeed that is what the Prime Minister said.

Their suggestions for how this Bill can be improved and how their lives can ultimately be improved are extremely important. I agree that the legislative committee should travel throughout Atlantic Canada and get the input of people living there. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Member of Parliament from Atlantic Canada and one who is excited about the agency and its creation, it is my pleasure to address some comments today to Bill C-103.
Bill C-103 establishes six basic operating principles of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency; consultation, decisionmaking in the region, emphasis on small and medium enterprises, adapting regional development programs to regional needs, creating the environment for business and economic growth to flourish with flexibility.
Consultation is a key part of the Government's fresh approach to regional development. Since the formation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency was announced on June 6 there has been extensive consultation in every area of Atlantic Canada with provincial governments, businessmen, and representatives of labour groups.
The consultation process means that the key regional development decisions will be made with the advice of true experts on regional problems and regional opportunities, the people who live and work in Atlantic Canada and care about Atlantic Canada. It is the small and medium enterprises which create the jobs in our economy and Atlantic Canada is no different. The agency will build on that job-creating ability of small and medium enterprises to create and sustain the economic growth Atlantic Canada needs. Through the extensive consultation process, the agency will be able to adapt broad federal regional development programs to best meet the needs of Atlantic Canada.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The agency marks the end of regional development policies and programs imposed from outside the region. An environment will be created in which business can grow and prosper. The agency will encourage an understanding throughout the region of the very important role of business to the economy, and create an atmosphere in which men and women of ideas can turn their ideas to the economic benefit of the region.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in order to prepare for the announcement of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, had asked Dr. Donald Savoie, an Atlantic Canadian, to do consultation work throughout Atlantic Canada. Mr. Savoie was the head of the Canadian Institute for Research on Regional Development at the University of Moncton, and he has a broad extensive background not only in regional development but also dealing with Government. At one time I believe he served as special assistant to now Senator Romeo Leblanc. He was to meet with other Atlantic Canadians, businessmen, provincial governments, university officials, labour representatives to discuss how regional development could be more effective in Atlantic Canada.
As a result of that fresh look at regional development programs, we have the creation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Perhaps the most important result of this extensive consultation process has been the creation of a network of men and women throughout Atlantic Canada who know about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, who know the ACOA staff and who know they can use ACOA to improve the region's economy. That is the sole purpose of ACOA. It is, this Parliament willing, the legislative purpose of the agency as set out in Clause 4, "to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada and, more particularly, to enhance the growth of earned incomes and employment opportunities".
ACOA will help improve the region's economy by taking responsibility from existing regional development programs and adding new programs. The Prime Minister has promised to maintain the present level of funding for existing programs like the Atlantic Enterprise Program, Industrial Regional Development Program, Enterprise Cape Breton and the Economic Regional Development Agreements, about $196 million a year.
The Government is also committed to putting $1.05 billion in new money into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency over the next five years, which is roughly $200 million a year. This means ACOA will administer almost $400 million each year in regional development funds in Atlantic Canada for the next five years.
Just how that $400 million a year will be used is currently stated in Clause 4 and Clause 12 of Bill C-103, which outline the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and what it will do. Clause 4 states that "the purpose of the agency is to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada

January 19, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
and, more particularly, to enhance the growth of earned incomes and employment opportunities".
Clause 12 adds to that, saying that the agency will place: ''particular emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises, through policy, program and project development and implementation and through advocacy of the interests of Atlantic Canada in national economic policy, program and project development and implementation".
The human meaning of that dry, legal language is that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will develop the most important resource of Atlantic Canada, the people of Atlantic Canada.
The commitment to the people of the region is the key part, the important part of the Government's fresh approach to regional development. Regional development must be based on local involvement, must be based on the local economy, must be developed mainly by local people who are those with the most intimate knowledge of what will work and with the greatest stake in making development work.
This is the first real regional economic development policy that will not be dependent upon ideas that are made and formulated in Ottawa. It will not be, once again, the flow of ideas from Ottawa because that is what Ottawa thinks is best for Atlantic Canada. This agency will utilize the innovative thinking, the entrepreneurial spirit and ideas of Atlantic Canadians who know best what the Atlantic Canada economy needs and what will work in Atlantic Canada.
This Bill gives Atlantic Canadians the tools to develop their economy in a way that no previous development Act has ever done. It throws out a challenge to Atlantic Canadians to show that they, with their enterprise and their initiative, can do the job.
We know Atlantic Canadians can create their own opportunities. As a Member of Parliament from Atlantic Canada, I can assure the House that we need and want the opportunity for economic growth. We want to use our entrepreneurial talents. This Bill gives us the financial resources and the leeway to utilize our entrepreneurial talents, to make it work in Atlantic Canada.
Let there be no doubt that there is entrepreneurial talent in Atlantic Canada. Between 1978 and 1985, Atlantic Canadian entrepreneurs created 20,000 new enterprises, each with fewer than 100 employees, to give the region 70,000 small and medium sized enterprises.
This is not regional development imposed from Ottawa. It is regional development with roots in the region.
To ensure that the purpose of the Bill will be met and that the agency will help Atlantic Canada direct its own economic development and build on its human resources and its abundant natural resources on the land and in the sea, Senator Murray will be advised by a 19-member board of men and women from and of the region.
When examining the board, we must take into consideration the role which these 19 people have been assigned. The role of the board is to give policy advice. It will direct the staff to conduct studies and formulate policy options. It will review program proposals and innovative or unusual projects, and will recommend policies or decisions to the Minister. The Minister retains the executive power of decision-making but will be strongly guided by the recommendations of the board which consists of these 19 members from Atlantic Canada.
While most people have understood and welcomed the creation of this board, and the strong advocacy capacity, some have suggested that a decision-making board which would focus on projects and specific cases where it could make final decisions, would be more appropriate.
This argument misses the point. Of course, the group of people on the ACOA board could make good decisions on specific cases. They have the experience to do so, but if they had to examine even a partial share of the hundreds of cases that come before ACOA they would have to become full-time employees of ACOA. Even then, there would be no time for the vital job of guiding the broad policy developments of the agency.
Of course, the board will have all the information on the cases and project decisions of ACOA and will comment on these program delivery decisions as appropriate. Indeed, this kind of independent, objective review of program results will be a big contribution by the board to the operations of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities agency.
The agency will be an advocate for Atlantic Canada, defining and promoting the interests of Atlantic Canada at regional and national levels; promoting an Atlantic perspective and ensuring that Atlantic Canada gets fair and reasonable consideration, and a fair and reasonable share of the benefits from national policies and programs.
Following the Prime Minister's announcement about the establishment of the agency in St. John's, Newfoundland, on June 6, responsibility for economic and regional development agreements was transferred to Senator Murray and ACOA. Under this Bill, the strategy and management of the ERDAs is a responsibility of the agency.
Discussions are now being held on a new series of economic and regional development agreements with each of the four Atlantic provinces.
Clause 6(2) of the Bill says that the Minister for ACOA may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into agreements with the government of any province or provinces in Atlantic Canada respecting the carrying out of any programs or project of the agency.
Clause 13(h) gives the agency power to enter into contracts, memoranda of understanding or other arrangements in the name of the agency.
January 19, 1988

Clause 18 of the Bill deals with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Board, made up of 19 people from Atlantic Canada, as I mentioned. Their main job is to assist the agency in the exercise of its powers and performance of its duties and functions. New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have five members each on the board, and Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland have four members each. Members are owners and operators of small and medium-sized enterprises, representatives of provincial governments, regional development commissions, and of labour.
1 have a list of the members of the agency. I want to mention some of the occupations which describe the broad range represented by the board of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. One board member is an acting chairman of the cabinet secretariat from the Province of New Brunswick. Another is president of Canada East Tours, located in Bathurst. Another individual is the owner of Atlantic Mini-Fridge Company, located in Moncton. This person used to work for the old Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and saw some of the benefits government programs were offering to Atlantic Canada. He took the initiative, formed his own company, and has done extremely well. He has offered his expertise and experience to the advantage of all Atlantic Canadians, by serving on the board of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
The President of Assumption Mutual Life, located in Edmundston with headquarters in Moncton, is another member of the board. The regional librarian for the Saint John Regional Library is another member of the board as is a member of the Canadian Advisory Board from Marsh McLennan in Halifax.
Despite some of the criticisms we heard in the House yesterday, another member of the board is the international representative of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers located in Sydney, Nova Scotia.
Another is partner in MCS Ventures located in Halifax. There is the executive director of the Eastern Shore Development Commission in Halifax County. There is the President of Stewart Restaurant in New Glasgow. Prince Edward Island is represented by a director from the Atlantic Ventures Trust in Charlottetown. There is the president and general manager of M.F. Schurman Limited in Summerside. It is represented by a well known lawyer from Prince Edward Island, and from the Government side, the secretary to the policy board of the Government of Prince Edward Island. Newfoundland is also well represented with the manager of the National Life of Canada located in St. John's, the Assistant Deputy Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs, the president of General Industries Limited and the president of North Limited, which is located in Goose Bay, Labrador. These people have offered to share their talent and expertise to help Atlantic Canadians take full use of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Since that board was appointed on August 31, a great deal of activity has taken place with respect to Atlantic Canada and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The agency spends a great deal of time addressing itself to Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. That is a topic I will leave to a representative from Cape Breton. I am sure they will be able to give a first-hand impression of what Bill C-103 will do with respect to the Cape Breton Enterprise Corporation and what it offers to the people of Cape Breton.
I have outlined briefly what this Bill will do for Atlantic Canada and Atlantic Canadians once it is passed by Parliament. Since June 6 when the Prime Minister announced the formation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency there have been consultation meetings held all across Atlantic Canada. A head office has been established in Moncton and certainly as the Member of Parliament for Moncton, I can tell Members that it is a pleasing thought to us to have in Moncton a headquarters of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency which, in essence, is really a national agency.
We welcome the people who will be employed in that agency. We are sure they will find Moncton an excellent place to work, to live and to bring up a family, and possibly, after successful years with the agency, an excellent place to retire.
Offices have been set up in every provincial capital. Staff has been hired and work has been done on a policy framework for the agency which has resulted in the Bill before us here today.
ACOA has been administering and delivering existing regional development programs since it was created. It has cut red tape and streamlined the delivery process to get funds to those who need them in the shortest time possible. Over 90 per cent of the applications under AEP, IRDP and ECB can now be directly approved by the regional vice-president. This has made the approval process much simpler and faster.
In the six-and-a-half months since the agency was established, it has approved 451 applications and authorized $68 million in contributions to the Atlantic Enterprises Program. These approvals have meant that business has been able to create 1,704 new jobs and has enabled these businesses to retain 2,648 additional jobs. We are now asking Parliament to give us the authority to do the full and complete job we must do to bring Atlantic Canada into full partnership with Canada's economic life.
This Bill creates an agency which will allow Atlantic Canadians to make decisions about their economic future. This Bill creates an agency which Atlantic Canada can use as an instrument to mold so that Atlantic Canadians can seize the opportunities of the future. It does not repeat the mistakes of the past. It does not expect Atlantic Canadians to adapt to programs best suited for central or western Canada. In fact, this Bill gives Atlantic Canadians, through the agency, the

January 19, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
tools needed to adapt national programs to meet the specific needs of the region.
The agency takes into account the dramatically different economy, industrial base, environment and cultures of the Atlantic Canada region in a way that is fresh and exciting. We have targeted, in particular, small and medium sized enterprises, those locally owned and locally managed, as the best way to improve economic performance in Atlantic Canada. Smaller enterprises have a proven record of creating new permanent jobs. The job of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is to encourage local growth. We know this can best be done by increasing the number of small and medium sized enterprises operating and flourishing in Atlantic Canada.
ACOA will develop the abundant talent and ability of Atlantic Canadians. This is a new partnership for Atlantic Canada of private and public sectors, a development partnership with improved and faster decision-making authority. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane), about those who dare to criticize the formulation and, indeed, the implementation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency was a character assassination which I do not believe is becoming of that Member.

The fight to lessen regional disparities did not begin in September of 1984. Policies of the past were put forward with the same hope and desire to lessen those disparities before September of 1984. Unfortunately, many of those programs were not as successful as one would have hoped.
However, it is worth noting the effect, as was indicated by the so-called expert in the person of Dr. Donald Savoie, who submitted a report to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in May of 1987, that some of the previous policies have had on lessening regional disparities, particularly those in Atlantic Canada. I do not subscribe, nor do Members of my Party subscribe, to the statements made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister responsible in this House for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, when he said that all programs of previous Governments were bad, did not address the issues and were not successful.
1 remind the Minister and, indeed, all Members opposite, of what Mr. Savoie said in the introduction of his report that he gave to the Prime Minister. He stated that, "If we have learned anything about the problem of regional development during the past 30 years in Canada, it is surely that there are no panaceas." That must be the same for this particular agency in that it, too, is no panacea.
It is also worthwhile to note that on pages six, seven and eight of this report to the Prime Minister he writes about regional equity in public services. He states:
Federal transfers to the provinces and to individuals in Atlantic Canada over the years have had an important impact on the economic structure of the region. Unfortunately, this fact has been too often overlooked. By concentrating on standard economic indicators of employment and per capita income, we have never focused sufficiently on the important progress that has been made in the region in recent years.
Those are the words of Dr. Donald Savoie set out in his report to the Prime Minister in May of 1987.
The report further states:
Federal transfers to provincial governments and to individuals have enabled the Atlantic provinces to close the gap with the other regions on a number of fronts. By 1979-80, the total fiscal capacity of the Atlantic provinces fell within a relatively narrow range, 85-99 per cent of the national average. This brought the Atlantic provinces much closer to the national average of provincial expenditures per capita in 1979 than they were in 1962. Federal finance officials report still more progress in recent years with all four Atlantic provinces now close to 95 per cent of the national average (after all federal transfers).
Increased provincial expenditures can indicate improved public services, as has been the case in Atlantic Canada.
He goes on to quote and itemize some of those.
On page 7 of the report it states:
Federal transfer payments have not only increased the capacity of provincial governments to provide services to their residents but have also enabled individual Canadians in lhavc-not' regions to acquire basic household
necessities. Regional disparities in this respect, extremely wide twenty years
ago, are now virtually non-existent.
Dr. Savoie gives the example that Newfoundland moved from 38.3 per cent in 1961 to 97.1 per cent of the national average in 1981 for the indicator "households with refrigerators", and the report goes on and on.
The policies of the past, although they have not met our expectations, hopes, or desires, in a way have tried to alleviate some of those problems. I wish to put that on the record in order that all Members will be cognizant of what has taken place, and indeed of the words of Dr. Donald Savoie, the expert, as indicated by Members opposite.
This debate in the Conservative Party has raged on from 1982, through 1983 and 1984 leading up to the federal election where the Conservatives won with an overwhelming majority, and 1 believe the largest majority in Atlantic Canada for quite some time. That majority was predicated on the fact that they and they alone had the answers, or many of the answers with regard to the lessening of regional disparity in Atlantic Canada.
That was prior to September of 1984. Many Members on this side of the House, and many residents of Atlantic Canada, automatically assumed that the Government of the day, knowing full well the difficulties and the problems of that particular region, would have a program or a series of programs which could address the fundamental problems in the Atlantic economy.
From September 4, 1984 we had to wait more than two years until October 1, 1986 for the Government to put some words on paper with regard to regional disparities. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, those were the words which were contained in the Throne Speech by the governing Party. That was October 1, 1986, and here we are in January, 1988 now dealing with a Bill which, if one goes by the words and sentiments expressed by the Minister of Transport responsible for Atlantic Canada opportunities, will be our panacea. It has been almost four full years before the problem of regional disparities in Atlantic Canada are addressed in a substantive manner.
I suggest to you, Sir, that perhaps the critics of this agency may have a point in that we are on the route or the path to a general election only months ahead, and that this is mere window dressing on which to run the next federal election.
The critics, as commented by the Hon. Member for Moncton whom I believe was rather unfair in his assessment of the criticism coming from that particular organization in Atlantic Canada, are real, because our expectations, our hopes and dreams of lessening disparity have been fueled by a governing Party which has repeatedly stated that it would have the answers and the programs to address those most serious situations.
The time lag is one major problem. But let us look at the moneys that the Government of Canada is committing to
January 19, 1988

regional economic development in Atlantic Canada. Much has been said of the billion dollars. In fact, the Prime Minister has gone on record to talk about new money to the tune of $1 billion. Canadians, and particularly Atlantic Canadians, ought to be reminded that since 1984 the Government has reduced the financial wherewithal in terms of regional disparities by approximately $1 billion annually for a deficit or a reduction in regional development expenditures of $3 billion. The Government has now stated that in place of that it will allot $200 million annually, adding up over five years to $1 billion. That is another example of the lack of sincerity and lack of political will of the governing Party and its huge majority.
One would have to conclude the ineffectiveness of the whopping majority of Conservative Members from Atlantic Canada, and in particular the Cabinet representations, in what we are receiving in Atlantic Canada in view of those obvious, startling revelations in terms of the reduction of moneys allocated toward regional disparities.

I
I say to you, Mr. Speaker that that is not negligence by the Government of Canada, that is not negligence by the Prime Minister or the Atlantic Ministers in that Cabinet, it is gross negligence that they would treat a region of this country with such disrespect by making it wait for almost four years before introducing legislation to address the seriousness of regional disparities, and thereafter substantially reducing the moneys being allocated to reduce regional disparities in our region. government benches say nothing of the disrespect that this Government has shown to our region.

DEVCO will retain a clear commercial mandate to continue the coalmining

Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The promises have been ignored because the major objective of this Conservative Government has been its insistence that before anything can be done to help the people of Canada and the many regions of Canada which need assistance the deficit which it says is unnecessarily high must be reduced.
When looking at this Bill, an Act to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, we must keep in mind that since its election in 1984 this Conservative Government has reduced funding for federal Government programs in Atlantic Canada by $1.5 billion annually. Now it proposes, if and when this Bill is passed, to give this new agency $1.5 billion, not $1.5 billion annually but $1.5 billion over a period of five years. That is just $200 million a year.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) talked about Atlantic Canada before the election he promised that the Conservative Government would pump new money into Atlantic Canada. We see that instead of pumping new money into Atlantic Canada the Conservative Government has reduced very substantially the funding for Atlantic Canada.
The objective of this agency, as outlined by Senator Murray, is that it will concentrate its efforts almost entirely on the private sector helping individual companies get going. I wish that members on the government side would look at the experience in the United States, particularly in the have-not states, the southern states of the U.S.A. They have come to realize that low wages will not produce jobs, certainly not good jobs. They have come to realize that they cannot compete in a meaningful way, in a way that will help their people as long as the infrastructure which they provide is so poor compared to the western states, the northern states and the central states. States like Mississippi have the lowest per capita expenditure on education. Sewer and water systems are poor, electric power rates are high and roads and bridges are in poor shape. These have-not states cannot compete and they have begun to realize that.
The Canadian Government ignores that evidence from the United States and ignores the evidence we should have accumulated in Canada by now. Without providing the required basic infrastructure, physical and human, Atlantic Canada will not be able to improve and certainly will not be able to compete with more prosperous areas in Canada.
Under this Conservative Government the commitment to regional development and assistance to Atlantic Canada has declined substantially. I talked about the $1.5 billion reduction annually for Atlantic Canada. Let us put that in more precise terms. Explicit regional development expenditure in 1984-85 for all of Atlantic Canada was about $230 million. That is just 15 per cent of the unemployment insurance payments for the area. Expenditures under DRIE's industrial incentive programs have decreased in real terms from $9 a person in the 1969-74 period to $4 a person for the 1984-86 period. Expenditures under the GDA and ERDA programs has declined
from $16 a person for the period 1974-79 to $14 in 1984-86. Even the Conservative Government of Newfoundland has estimated that a minimum requirement for funding this agency so it could do its job properly would require an expenditure of $366 million a year instead of the $200 million which is being put forward by this Bill.
1 was struck by some of the remarks made yesterday by the Conservative Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). He said in part that this agency will build up the research capabilities of the area's universities to ensure that regional enterprise is fostered. We can build on the excellent universities in the area, he said. Then he compared the large scale unemployment in Atlantic Canada with the New England States which have a low rate of unemployment.
The Hon. Member from York-Sunbury and other Conservative Members should ask why there is that difference. First, the United States, under the Reagan administration, has been involved in a tremendous and major increase in expenditures for the production of armaments. Even the Conservative Government which is proposing to build nuclear submarines, tanks and ships could not visualize a similar rate of expansion for the building of armaments in this country.
There is another very good reason. The universities in the New England States, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard University, Boston University, and the University of Massachusetts have been very heavily involved in scientific research and development funded to a large extent by federal and state Governments. That research and development has led to the spin-off of a large number of new companies involved in high technology areas. We have nothing like that in Canada and we are not likely to get anything like that, given this Government's approach to research and development.
I remind Members of Parliament that before the 1984 election the present Prime Minister castigated the then Liberal Government because Canada's expenditure for scientific research and development was one of the lowest of any of the countries belonging to the OECD and Japan. While other countries were allocating 2 per cent to 2.5 per cent of their Gross National Product to scientific research and development, Canada's rate of expenditures was just about 1.3 per cent, half of what other countries were doing.
The present Prime Minister quite properly castigated the then Liberal Government and promised that a Conservative Government would double the rate of expenditures to 2.5 per cent, but what is the record and the reality, Mr. Speaker? The reality is, as the Prime Minister had to admit at the recent Conference on Scientific Research and Technology, that this year, after over three years of Conservative Government, we are still devoting only 1.3 per cent of our Gross National Product to scientific research and development.
What happens as a result of that? Canada is the only major industrialized country with trade deficits in all of the major high technology groups including aerospace, data processing machines, drugs and electronic equipment. Canada is also
January 19, 1988

failing to educate sufficient numbers of scientists and engineers who might sustain the necessary economic transformation. If we do not have that transformation, we will have more unemployment, more people working at low wages because the resource-based industries on which we have always depended are facing increasing competition from Third World countries with much lower wage rates than we have, and our resources are, to a large extent, being rapidly depleted.
In an OECD survey of the number of scientists and engineers per 10,000 people in the labour force, Canada had just one-third as many as Japan, less than half of the number in the United States and just over half the number in West Germany. There are approximately 50,000 businesses in Canada that depend on technology and only 2.5 per cent of the total, about 1,250, are involved in any research and development. Contrast that with the United States where there are
15,000	firms spending $110 billion annually on research and development at a rate of three times ours as a percentage of domestic product.
At the recent conference on scientific research and technology the Prime Minister announced that the Government would be allocating another $250 million a year to the universities for scientific research and development. That sounds very good until you compare that announcement with the announcement made just about the same time that the private sector companies in the U.S.A. involved in the production of computer chips are, this year, investing the same amount of money, $250 million, into a new research facility located in one city in the United States, that of Austin, Texas. That is only a small illustration of how far behind we are falling.
When the former Liberal Government announced a cutback and limits on transfers to post-secondary education under the Established programs Financing program, the then Conservative Opposition voted against the proposal. What has the present Government done? In the Budget which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced in 1985 we saw a proposed further cumulative loss to the provinces of nearly $6 billion between 1986-87 and 1990-91 of which $1.6 billion represents losses to post-secondary education institutions across the country.
What does that mean for post-secondary institutions in Atlantic Canada? From 1986 to 1990 the universities will lose; Newfoundland, $37 million a year; Prince Edward Island, $8 million; Nova Scotia, $55 million; and New Brunswick, $45 million. That is almost $200 million right there. These reductions will severely compromise the ability of the universities to carry out the research and teaching they should be doing, particularly since these universities have already, over the years of Liberal Governments, had their funding reduced.
We see a similar situation with the granting councils. The Government recently attempted to hide its negligence in funding university research by announcing a matching grant
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
scheme. In February, 1986, the Minister of Finance announced that the Government would match private sector contributions to the three granting councils up to a maximum of 6 per cent annually.
Even the most optimistic projections on the dollar value of the matching grant schemes indicate that funding to the granting councils will be only marginally increased over the frozen base budget level. If you compare the matching grant scheme to the proposed five-year plans prepared by the granting councils themselves, there is a short-fall of hundreds of millions of dollars. The five-year plans that the granting councils developed were to meet the research goals and technology development strategies outlined by the federal Government, so the continued inadequate funding is inexcusable and tragically short-sighted. That means that the claims which the Member for York-Sunbury and other Conservative Members have made will simply will not materialize.
Let us look at the granting councils. In May of last year Dr. Bois, the President of the Medical Research Council, told the Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare that the Medical Research Council had to implement a whole range of Draconian measures to cope with the current fiscal crisis. Among the measures that they adopted was that the approval rate of new operating grants from the February, 1987 competition was limited to approximately 25 per cent, even below the usual low approval rate of 30 per cent, and actual funding of the approved applications was delayed from July to October forcing disruptions in many planned research projects.
One of the areas in which new and important discoveries which will save hundreds and thousands of lives are being made is the field of medical research. Whole new industries are being established as a result of these discoveries. Just when that is happening all around the world the Conservative Government cuts back and freezes funding for the Medical Research Council.
Let us look at the National Research Council. Before the Prime Minister became Prime Minister he said that the National Research Council, which acts as Canada's main research laboratory, needed a funding increase of at least 20 per cent to bring its budget up to $400 million. That was four years ago. In May, 1987, the President of the National Research Council told the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology that the NRC budget had just reached $408 million. However, he also pointed out that in the preceding 12 months there had been $31 million worth of decreases at the NRC including a $4 million cut-back in science funding in British Columbia and $19 million in reductions to the NRC's regular programs.
At the same time as it is ignoring well-established and productive research at the NRC and University Granting Council the Government is plunging headlong into the vague area of space research, where there is no demonstrable track record, without the approval or agreement of any reputable scientific advisory committee.

January 19, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
Let us look at some of the areas in which government research has been important, for example, the business of food production and utilization of agricultural products, which is the most important and largest industry in Canada and is very important to Atlantic Canada. Twenty-five per cent of Canadians are involved in producing, researching, processing, servicing, and other parts of the food industry. It should be obvious that research in this area is tremendously important. In 1970 Canada's agricultural expenditures were 3.7 per cent of the total federal expenditures. By 1978 they had dropped to 2.4 per cent and are now only 1.9 per cent of total federal expenditures. Of this, only 10.9 per cent was devoted to agricultural research. In fact, between 1985 and 1987 federal expenditures in science and technology activities in agriculture declined by over $14 million.
Let us look at forestry, another area important to Atlantic Canada. Forest products industries represent one of Canada's largest industrial sectors accounting for about one job in every seven. It is very sad, therefore, to report that Canada is the only Government in the western world with a forestry ministry but no forestry research capabilities because the former Conservative Government in 1979 sold the forestry lab.
I think I have indicated very clearly what has happened under this Government. I will summarize what has happened in the way of cuts in university research funding. From EPF $5.5 billion nationally will have been cut by 1990. Important cuts have been made to universities in Atlantic Canada which have always been under-funded.
As my colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), has indicated, this is a major effort to flimflam the public. It is another public relations effort to convince people that the Government, which has in fact done so many things to hurt Atlantic Canada, is finally going to rectify the mistakes it made and give Atlantic Canada the help it needs. The help it is getting is substantially less than the help it got under the former Liberal Government, which help was itself inadequate.
For all those reasons we intend to vote against this Bill.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker was kind enough to refer to my remarks in the House yesterday, and for that I thank him. Being mentioned by such a distinguished and highly respected parliamentarian is a very distinct honour for me and I am very grateful to him.
He mentioned in particular my allusion to the locomotive economy aspect that could be adopted by Atlantic Canada if we are able to trade more freely with the State of Maine and learn lessons from the way they have built on their great universities led by Harvard and MIT. He correctly points out that Canada's ability to purchase military installations and armaments is certainly not comparable to that of the United States. I should point out to him, however, that in the Province of New Brunswick we have the largest army training area in Canada and it is the largest employer of skilled and semi
skilled persons in central New Brunswick. We also have more defence installations per capita than in any other part of Canada. These bases provide a large number of jobs.
The Hon. Member mentioned forestry and the lack of research. I should tell him that under construction in the City of Fredericton is the largest and most modern research facility in forestry in Canada. It is called the Forestry Complex. It is a product of the Government of Canada, being the largest contributor of funds, along with the Maritime Provinces and the University of New Brunswick. It opens a window on research for the vital forest industry which, as the Hon. Member mentions, employs one out of seven people directly and indirectly, and is a leading industry and stimulant of employment in the Province of New Brunswick and indeed Atlantic Canada.
He may also be interested to know that the Government of Canada is setting in place an incubation centre for science, a science mall to test new inventions and spin-off new industries. ACOA is negotiating with the University of New Brunswick for an international marketing function to take full advantage of the great stimulant to Atlantic Canada in freer trade, which I believe his Party also opposes.
CADCAM, Computer Assisted Design and Computer Assisted Manufacturing Centre at the University of New Brunswick, and the Advancement of the Research Productivity Council are all efforts of this Government to build on science and on technology and research to create jobs in Atlantic Canada. I am sure the Hon. Member will be very pleased to hear that before he gave us his wise advice we had already heeded and implemented it.
The Repap Mill which has been built in the riding of the Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Jardine) has cost several hundred millions of dollars, most of it coming from the private sector. This does not appear in our budgetary estimates or public accounts, but it is part of the Government's attempt to get the private sector to invest in the area by inducing them with incentives and encouraging them to create jobs. That has created several hundred jobs in the area of highest unemployment in the Province of New Brunswick.
1 am sure the Hon. Member will be pleased to see that we are already implementing many of the very wise and excellent suggestions he has made in his remarks and for which 1 would very much like to commend him.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I am pleased to be advised that the Government has instituted a number of programs which will help improve the deplorable record in the area of scientific research and development. However, I remind the Member for York-Sunbury that, according to the Prime Minister, we are still only devoting 1.3 per cent of our Gross National Product to scientific research and development. That is only half of what most other countries are doing.
January 19, 1988

Let me refer to the forestry industry. That is one of the largest employers in Canada and is a very important industry in Atlantic Canada. Our record is a disgrace. For every two trees cut down, at most only one tree is replanted. Even industry sources are telling us that some 25 years from now the distance from which companies will have to bring wood to their mills will make it uneconomic to keep their plants and mills operating.
Let us consider the example of other countries. Sweden has had social democratic government for 45 of the last 50 years. Most of the forests in that country are owned privately, but that social democratic government-which some Tories believe is absolutely opposed to free enterprise-co-operated with the private owners of the forest lands so that for every tree which is cut another tree is planted. Furthermore, they have made major efforts to develop new, better and faster growing trees, some of which they obtained from British Columbia. They are growing and planting trees in the millions.
Most of the forests in this country are owned and controlled either by the federal or provincial governments. These governments, which almost invariably believe in the free enterprise system, have done virtually nothing to insist that the private companies to which they give licences plant a tree for every tree they are permitted to cut.
The profits of these companies over two generations have been astronomical. Yet what have they done for this country? As a result of their negligence and refusal to co-operate in planting trees to replace those that they cut down, they have brought the industry to the point where, according to industry sources themselves, we will be facing a major catastrophe in the next couple of generations.
While I am happy that the Government has taken some hesitant steps in the right direction, there is still a long way to go. The Conservative Government is fixated in the belief that it must cut back the deficit, which is caused to a large extent by the fact there is almost 10 per cent unemployment. These people are receiving Government assistance instead of being productive workers and paying income tax and sales taxes.
While 1 applaud some of the things the Government has done, it has a long way to go before it meets the needs of the people of Atlantic Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE NEW EARLY RETIREMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in August 1986, the Conservative Government abolished programs under which workers in the footwear, clothing and textile industry could take early retirement. It is now January 1988, and a new program is still not forthcoming.

subsubtopic: SITUATION IN MONTREAL'S EAST END-URGENT NEED FOR GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, in their replies to questions about the situation in Montreal's east end, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and the Prime Minister mentioned statistics that failed to reflect the real situation.

10,000	on welfare. Since 1985, Daoust-Lalonde Inc., La Parisette, SKD, Vickers and CIP have closed. subsubtopic: ISSUANCE OF OFFSHORE LOBSTER FISHING LICENCES IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the Government has shown it cannot live up to the trust of Canadians. Last week the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) issued four offshore lobster licences to companies in Nova Scotia. The Premier of Nova Scotia has also objected to the awarding and issuing of these licences.
The Lobster Advisory Council, a group which advises the Minister on such matters, has come out against the awarding and issuing of these licences. In fact last Friday its members threatened to resign unless the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans cancelled these licences.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the great news continues. A recent Decima poll indicates that free trade with the United States is gaining support and now has the favour of the majority of Canadians. This is good news for those of us who believe that it is just what the doctor ordered for the Canadian consumer.
The Economic Council of Canada has predicted a decline in the consumer price index which could give between $700 and $1,000 in additional purchasing power to the average Canadian. In Alberta we would call that substantial, and recognize it as a means of insulating our economy against a recurrence of the dark days of the early 1980s.
Many Canadians already buy extensively in the United States. The duty they pay at Customs upon their return amounts to additional tax and lost savings. Eventually free trade will eliminate these duties while encouraging more Americans to come north.
It is high time for all Members to get onside and to tell Canadians the truth about free trade. It will mean lower prices, wider selection, and higher quality goods for everybody. The bottom line is more money in the pockets of the average consumer.

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF PROVINCIAL ECOLOGY LAW IN CASE OF FEDERAL INFRACTION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government cannot set itself above provincial legislation on the environment, especially now that as a result of Bill C-74, the federal Government is becoming increasingly dependent on provincial governments to protect the environment. It therefore comes as something of a shock that the federal Government should challenge the application of provincial legislation in a case where there has been a federal violation of that law.

Where is co-operative federalism when we really need it in the field of the environment? This is an absolutely deplorable situation. In Bill C-74 the Government depends more than ever before on provincial Governments in the field of the environment. Then, when a provincial Government, in this case Ontario, applies the law the federal Government uses Crown immunity to hide behind its own infractions of provincial environmental laws.
We need tough, national standards on the environment. We need respect for provincial laws on the environment, on the part of the federal Government. The federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) ought to tell the Department of Justice not to proceed with an appeal and use legalistic ways to avoid its own responsibility.

subsubtopic: SENATE'S DELAY IN PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each day hundreds of individuals who wish to circumvent Canada's immigration laws use fraudulent methods to gain access into Canada. This assault on our immigration system is the result of 20 years of Liberal neglect.
The Government acted by passing Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 which would curb the abuse and at the same time send out a clear message that individuals who lie and cheat would no longer have access to Canada. Yet this legislation has not become law due to the lack of the Liberal Senate's approval.
The Liberal Senate seems determined to assure the survival of the old system. This brings us to an interesting juncture. The two opposition Parties which used every means to discredit Bill C-55 and Bill C-85 are now demanding action on the PLO terrorist who lied his way into Canada. Had these Bills become law this terrorist would be denied the claim of refugee status as an avenue of appeal.
Another terrorist, Francesco Piperno, used the refugee route to remain in Canada for 10 years. When he decided to leave there was still no decision on his case.
Therefore, the bluster shown by the Opposition is hollow. It should be directing its thunder toward the Senate where the laws demanded by the Canadian people are presently stalled.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-106, an Act to provide for the resumption of grain handling operations at the port of Prince Rupert, British Columbia, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to the Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my unhappy task to inform the House that once again the parties to a collective agreement have failed to accept their responsibility to resolve their differences. I refer to Prince Rupert Grain Limited and the Grain Workers Union Local 333 whose dispute has deprived Canadians of an important grain export facility. There is no indication or reasonable expectation that the dispute between the parties will be resolved in the foreseeable future, notwithstanding the fact that a sensible, formal proposal was placed before the parties which would have settled this dispute and avoided the intervention of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult for a Minister of Labour to have to make such an assessment. Our system of free collective bargaining is founded on certain fundamental principles of democracy which our society relies on to resolve differences between competing interests.
Like many of the relationships which we each encounter in our lives, labour relations are adversarial relations. Yet the basic principles which govern these relations generally ensure that these competing interests are reconciled without irreparable harm to the parties involved or to innocent third-parties.
Such is not the case in Prince Rupert. In Prince Rupert there are two opposing interest groups, Prince Rupert Grain Limited, representing interests of six grain handling companies, and the Grain Workers Union Local 333, representing the 69 employees at the terminal. These parties have effectively said to the Canadian public, "We don't care about your interests or about collective bargaining. We will pursue our own private interests no matter what the cost to the national economy or to the overseas reputation of Canada".
This attitude is absolutely unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. It really does not matter who is right and who is wrong in this dispute, or even whether there is a right or wrong side to these issues. What is unacceptable is that the parties have made up their minds that they are not going to settle their differences through the democratic mechanisms which are provided by our Labour Code.
While both parties claim to have the interests of western farmers uppermost in mind, they both appear quite prepared to wait it out while the most efficient grain terminal in the country sits idle and Canada's international reputation as a reliable supplier of grain is destroyed.
In the most recent exercise aimed at resolving this work stoppage, I summoned the parties to Ottawa to meet under the auspices of the Associate Deputy Minister of Labour, Bill Kelly. Mr. Kelly's skills as a mediator are well known to all in this House, and he has justly earned his reputation. However, it did not take Mr. Kelly too long to conclude that the parties are so entrenched in their respective positions on the issues that no compromise was possible. He then made a formal proposal to them that they agree to submit their dispute to arbitration for final and binding resolution.
This is a method which has been used on three occasions in the past to resolve bargaining impasses in the grain terminals in Vancouver between the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators Association and the Grain Workers Union Local 333. It should have been crystal clear to the parties that Mr. Kelly's proposal was the obvious solution if they wished to avoid a legislated end to this dispute.
January 19, 1988

Even with this certain knowledge, they chose to continue their disregard for both the public interest and the principles of sound labour management relations. The union placed an unacceptable pre-condition on its acceptance of Mr. Kelly's proposal, while the employer rejected the proposal in its entirety. Indeed, the employer characterized the notion of arbitration on the key issue of manning as "irresponsible". One would have to wonder by what stretch of logic they considered it less than irresponsible to allow this dispute to continue.
Through their actions, the parties have effectively abrogated their responsibility to resolve their dispute, and made it quite clear that if the Prince Rupert Terminal is to be restored to operation, it will be through Government action, and not their own.
This is not what our collective bargaining system is all about. I find the attitude of these parties not only disappointing, but shameful. It is shameful in its disregard for the farmers of western Canada who are being held hostage to the intransigence of these two disputants, and shameful for its disregard of our collective bargaining system.
It is abhorrent for a Minister of Labour to have to recommend to Parliament that the right to be responsible for your own destiny be taken away from anyone, but the Prince Rupert Grain Terminal Limited and the Grain Workers Union Local 333 have left me with no other choice. This Government cannot allow the western economy to be further jeopardized by the private disputes of these parties.

For those who might question my assessment, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a moment to describe the efforts which have been made to promote a resolution of this dispute through the accepted collective bargaining process.

When the collective agreement which applied to this bargaining unit expired on December 31, 1983 the parties were aware that the new, highly automated terminal on Ridley Island would become operational during the life of the next collective agreement, and that there were transitional issues that would have to be faced. The parties agreed that issues that were common between Prince Rupert and Vancouver would be dealt with in the context of the bargaining that was taking place between the union and the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators Association.
These negotiations, which were conducted with the assistance of a conciliation officer and, subsequently, a conciliation commissioner, eventually concluded in May, 1985 with the signing of a three-year agreement. During the period of these negotiations, the new terminal in Prince Rupert was brought into operation. Although the issues which had been theoretical in 1983 were now very real, the parties remained unable to resolve them:
The conciliation commissioner my predecessor had appointed, Mr. Vince Ready, continued his efforts throughout the
Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
remainder of 1985, and in January, 1986 produced his report and recommendations for settlement. With certain reservations, the company accepted Mr. Ready's recommendations, but the union did not. In March, 1986, the Vancouver Regional Director of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, Mike Collins, was appointed as a mediator.
Meanwhile, the union pursued its efforts to have the scope of its bargaining unit expanded through applications to the Canada Labour Relations Board and the Federal Court of Appeal. Negotiations between the parties continued on an intermittent basis between April, 1986 and November, 1987, but neither side gave any evidence of its willingness to compromise on the fundamental issues. The union commenced strike action on December 9, 1987. Mediator Collins once again convened the parties, but to no avail, and on January 4, 1988 he terminated his involvement. Even at that point, I was unwilling to accept that so important a dispute could not be resolved through negotiation.
I summoned the parties to Ottawa to meet with my Associate Deputy Minister, Bill Kelly. Mr. Kelly explored every possible avenue for settlement of the dispute. When it became clear to him that neither side would make any compromise, he made a formal proposal to them which would, if accepted, have resolved the dispute and ensured the immediate resumption of terminal operations.
In addition to recommending that they implement the terms of the collective agreement now in effect for the Vancouver grain terminals, Mr. Kelly proposed that the parties voluntarily agree to submit their outstanding differences on manning in the grain centre, job classifications, and security personnel to an arbitrator for final and binding determination.
While the union agreed to the concept, they imposed an unacceptable condition on the process by insisting that a specific individual be named as the arbitrator. As anyone who has had any involvement in quasi-judicial proceedings is well aware, it is a fundamental principle that the individual or tribunal with the decision-making power must not only be impartial but must also appear to be impartial.
While I have the utmost respect for the individual proposed as arbitrator by the union, the very fact that he is the choice of one party to the dispute immediately raises apprehension in the mind of the other party. That individual's acceptability as an arbitrator is then seriously compromised. By stubbornly insisting on this condition, the union was effectively rejecting the mediator's proposal.
For its part the employer maintained its position that it would not voluntarily agree to submit these issues to a third party. In its reply to Mr. Kelly's proposal the employer claims that the subject of manning in the grain centre, which is the primary issue in dispute, was placed before the Canada Labour Relations Board and decided in the employer's favour. Thus, it

January 19, 1988
Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
contends that it would be irresponsible for it to agree to submit the issue to arbitration.
There is no logic to this response whatsoever. The matter which was placed before the CLRB for determination had to do with the inclusion or exclusion of certain positions from the bargaining unit. The board determined that the operations foremen in the grain centre are excluded from the scope of the union's bargaining certificate. However, at no time did the CLRB consider the issue of manning, which refers to the level of staffing that will exist in the grain centre. It is abundantly clear that the parties are unable or unwilling to resolve the manning issue through the negotiation process. If there is ever to be any hope of resolving this impasse, arbitration provides an ideal forum for an impartial hearing and determination of the interests which are involved.
Frankly the attitudes of this employer and this union are irresponsible. Given the extreme importance of Prince Rupert in Canada's grain export program, one might suspect that the parties are quite prepared to have Parliament make the difficult decision they are unwilling to make for themselves. Both sides are well aware that the Government cannot permit this terminal to remain idle for the months or years it might take before the parties decide that they should resolve their impasse.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the employees in Prince Rupert want to go back to work and get the grain moving again. I know that the western farmers desperately want the Prince Rupert terminal reopened. The will of the Canadian public, as expressed through their representatives here in this House, must in this case take precedence over the will and interests of the immediate participants to the dispute.

Let me turn now to the specific provisions of the Bill which will accomplish the resolution of this long-standing dispute. Not surprisingly, we are not asking Parliament to deviate from the proposal for settlement which the parties had an opportunity to accept voluntarily. The clear purpose of this approach is to send an unmistakable message to any negotiators who think that they can achieve more through legislation than through collective bargaining. Parliament will not reward parties who propel their disputes to our level for resolution.
In addition to providing for an immediate resumption of terminal operations, the Bill requires the parties to incorporate the terms of the agreement between the B.C. Terminal Elevator Operators Association and the Grain Workers Union in Vancouver into their collective agreement. In fact, this merely formalizes the existing informal arrangement in which the employer has been implementing any changes that have arisen from time to time as a consequence of the Vancouver agreement.
In respect of the three issues which caused the impasse in negotiations, the Bill calls for the appointment by the Minister
of Labour of any arbitrator to make a final and binding determination of these matters. A 45-day time limit is established for this process, subject to extension only if the parties mutually agree.
The public's patience with these parties is exhausted. They have had more than four years to resolve their differences. They have imposed the consequences of their dispute on western grain producers while continuing to reject every opportunity for a settlement through accepted dispute resolution mechanisms. The Government has an obligation to the farmers of the country to restore the export of their grain products through Prince Rupert, and this is precisely what we intend to do.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada, I would like to speak on Bill C-106, an Act to provide for the resumption of grain handling operations at the port of Prince Rupert, British Columbia, which has just been tabled. First, I wish to emphasize that we have co-operated with the Government to allow this Bill to reach the floor of the House of Commons as soon as possible. We agreed to forego the required 48-hour notice on the Order Paper and for the Bill to be introduced in the House of Commons today rather than Wednesday. We also agreed to the Bill being referred to a committee of the whole rather than a legislative or a standing committee, which would have made for a longer debate on this Bill.

If we have co-operated with the Government to try to ensure that the Bill passes the House of Commons quickly, it is because we think that it is about time the Government did something to get the grain moving again. Prairie farmers are already facing very difficult conditions. I am informed that on average the price of grain is about $110 per tonne, a level which is about half what it was five years ago. Needless to say, farmers are having a very rough time.
We are watching the United States and the European Economic Community systematically drive prices down. The American export enhancement program has a budget of $1.5 billion, which it is using to subsidize grain sales, sometimes in our traditional markets, and which has eaten away at some of our markets.
The only good news which prairie farmers have had recently is that sales have been good. The Canadian Wheat Board has been successful in selling grain. I am told that in 1986-87 we had record sales. However, it is one thing to conclude contracts with other countries to sell grain, and it is something else to deliver the commodity especially when grain terminals are at a standstill. The strike has cost us sales as the Canadian Wheat Board could not sign contracts for sales to be delivered prior to late March or early April.


January 19, 1988

Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier in what I consider to be a very competitive market was running the risk of being damaged.
This is what I mean when I describe the situation under which the farmers must live. This is what I mean when I say that it is about time that the Government did something. The elevators are clogged, the grain is not moving. The problem, though, is that the solution, the back-to-work legislation, is not exactly the solution we would have liked to have seen.
The Government is again indulging in what has become almost an addiction, and that is to wait until there is no other solution than back-to-work legislation. The Government seems to have fallen into the habit of wielding the billy stick whenever there is a labour dispute in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, other solutions were available to the Government. There were attempts to communicate with the parties involved, but there would surely have been a way to bring them to agree to binding arbitration instead of introducing back-to-work legislation.
In a press release last week, the Leader of the Official Opposition and Leader of the Liberal Party urged the Minister of Labour to meet last weekend with the two parties involved in the labour dispute which has shut down grain handling operations in the port of Prince Rupert to convince them to submit to binding arbitration. The Leader of the Opposition stated that the Minister should be ready to propose the name of an arbitrator to the two parties involved. However, the Minister chose not to meet with the parties involved and decided instead to introduce this Bill.

I am amazed at the fact that the Minister was not able to pass to the two parties this very simple message: "If you do not agree voluntarily to go into binding arbitration, it will be imposed upon you by back-to-work legislation". If that message had been passed properly, I am sure the two parties would have realized that an agreement had to come about and that it would be in their interests to agree voluntarily and have a say as to who the arbitrator would be. Now that will be imposed upon them. An arbitrator will be appointed, according to the Bill. Whether they like it or not, the parties will have to live with that individual who will be appointed.
Mr. Henry Kanes of Local 333 of the Grain Workers' Union had agreed in principle to go back to work voluntarily without a billy stick over his head. I agree that he was talking about a condition. He would have liked to have Mr. Justice Emmett Hall as the arbitrator, but he also said that someone else acceptable to his local could do as well. The employer did not agree to having Mr. Justice Emmett Hall as the arbitrator, but the employer did not disagree in principle with binding arbitration. In other words, the Minister could certainly have used words that would have helped these people understand
Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
that it would be better for them to agree voluntarily, first, on the principle of going back to work and, second, on the individual who would act as an arbitrator, and that if they did not do so, it would be imposed on them anyway. The Minister failed to say that. It is a failure on behalf of the Government to get the parties to understand what their interest in this dispute was.
I would like to turn to some of the details of the strike. This strike is not about money. This strike is about jobs. It is about the jobs of the people who staff the grain terminal at Prince Rupert.
I would like to quote a representative of the union, Mr. Henry Kanes of Grain Workers' Union Local 333, who said the following in a press release of last week:
This dispute is about jobs-union jobs. The sacrifices our members are making on the picket line are not for selfish reasons. It is so union members can share in the future world of computer technology and not become a relic of the past like the grain shovels we once used. We are intelligent enough to participate in the future. We already do it at other elevators.
A big part of the problem is that some jobs will be lost because of computerization. The union and the workers understand that, but they would like to see some of the remaining workers trained to work on those computers rather than having people come from large urban centres to operate these new electronic machines while the union members go on welfare or on unemployment insurance. That is what the strike is all about.
It is not an abusive use of the rights of workers when one considers that they have been out of a contract for four years. They waited for four years before going on strike last December, and they went on strike simply because they want the assurance that the people who will operate the modern, up-to-date grain handling equipment will be union members. I think it is only fair that they be given a fair chance to be trained to operate these computers rather than having computer operators come from the central part of Canada. That is the root of this strike. It is not strange that people would walk out to try to protect some of their basic rights as these people have done.
I mentioned earlier that the union membership was willing to return to work voluntarily without back-to-work legislation. I would like to quote again from the same press release put out by Local 333 of the Grain Workers' Union. Mr. Kanes said:
-two days after the strike began, I was approached by farmers and other organizations to return to work and accept an inquiry by former Supreme Court of Canada Justice Emmett Hall. I agreed to recommend this to our members with no conditions attached. The Company rejected this proposal from the farmers.
This must be put on the record so that the people of Canada who are watching these proceedings will know exactly what the score is.
After quoting these documents, I would say that the Government and the Minister failed to recognize the willingness expressed by the workers to try to avoid back-to-work legislation and to use methods that are more like the ones we

January 19, 1988
Adjournment Motion
would like to see used in this country, methods by which management and workers agree by themselves.
Let us take a look at this piece of legislation which, in my opinion, is what we have become accustomed to seeing in this Parliament. It is the standard back-to-work legislation. It extends the collective agreement until the end of 1989. It amends it by including the items that have been agreed to so far by the two parties. It appoints an arbitrator who will have to deal with three specific items; namely, the staffing of the grain terminal which is at issue, the classification of those workers and also the issue of whether or not security personnel will be included in the same bargaining unit. This arbitrator will have 45 days to complete his report unless the parties agree to an extension.
What we find abusive in this Bill are the same stiff penalties that we will never become accustomed to but that we have become accustomed to seeing in each and every piece of legislation which the Government tables in the House to bring workers back to work.
Let me take a quick run through this particular part of the Bill. For example, an officer of the union or representative of the employer who will contravene the present Act will be subject to a fine of no less than $10,000 and no more than $50,000 a day for an offence. We will be talking to this later when we come to the Committee of the Whole. On previous occasions, for instance in the postal strike, we have tried to educate the Minister to understand that one does not need penalties that high to get people to live up to their responsibilities in a country like Canada. Our judges and tribunals do not need a minimum penalty of $10,000 set out if the judge is to have the flexibility to determine what type of fine it will be.
We hope that this legislation nevertheless, and as unhappy as we are with its tabling, will get through the House as soon as possible because we want to get the grain moving again. We believe farmers have suffered enough from this breakdown in transportation of cereals. We hope the legislation will solve the problem. We have no hope that it will improve employer-employees relations generally in Canada because we think it is another bad example of the Government moving in and swinging the axe or the billy stick to try to put people up against the wall. We have no hope that it will change the attitude of the Government, but if we can get the grain moving again, at least we will accept that.
