subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-106, an Act to provide for the resumption of grain handling operations at the Port of Prince Rupert, British Columbia, I would like to state on behalf of our caucus that we are upset that this legislation was necessary. We believe that legislation of this nature, although perhaps not the exact legislation that we have before us, has indeed become necessary. During the negotiation and mediation process the two groups were unable to come to any satisfactory conclusion of negotiations. A long strike, although it helped to bring the issue to the public's mind, again did not result in the issue being resolved in a collective agreement.
We oppose the legislation as it is written not only because we find it unfortunate to have it in front of us but because the Government is insisting on retaining its regime of heavy fines, fines which quite often the employer can afford to pay but which are crippling to the individual if he or she ends up in a situation of being fined.
That is a problem and one of the major reasons we cannot support the legislation. Having said that, as you, Mr. Speaker, know, we have agreed to allow the legislation to pass the House of Commons. When we get into clause by clause study later on today we will be putting forward some amendments and voting against some parts of the legislation in an attempt to improve it. We believe that there are changes which could make this legislation better.
For Canadians there is no more difficult decision than whether to support workers who are trying to preserve their jobs or whether to support farmers who are trying to make sure that their grain or other commodities get to market. Canadians tend to sympathize with both groups. Some,
January 19, 1988

depending on where they live in this country, may support one group over the other, but in almost all cases, whether you are a farmer, a worker or involved in some endeavour, you recognize that the issues can be important to both the farmers and the workers. It is not an easy issue in legislation of this nature. You cannot really say that the farmers are at fault, because they are not at fault, they have legitimate concerns. You cannot say the workers are at fault, because they too have legitimate concerns. Legislation of this kind quite often creates a very emotional debate, a debate that sometimes gets quite unreasonable in the way Canadians treat each other.
I find it unfortunate that the two parties could not come to an agreement. In this case I think we have a situation where other methods were suggested to resolve this dispute. The appointment of former Justice Emmett Hall was not suggested just a week or two ago; it was suggested before Christmas. The union representative at that time said they would be willing to have the workers go back to work if former Justice Emmett Hall were appointed to arbitrate the issue. The union representatives went on to say that if it were not former Justice Emmett Hall, perhaps some other acceptable person could be brought in. They made that an option, an option which could have resolved the issue before Christmas or, at least if it did not resolve the issue, it could have resolved the work stoppage and allowed the grain to flow. But that was not done, Mr. Speaker. A month passed, mediation was attempted by the Associate Deputy Minister, Mr. Kelly, and that did not work. Now we are getting legislation in this House that is basically doing what could have been done a month ago.
At no time during that process did the employer agree to allow the issue in dispute to go to binding arbitration. As recently as yesterday, Party leaders were receiving telexes from the employer denying that the issue was whether or not the jobs in question should be part of the collective agreement. The employee was saying that that should not be dealt with by an arbitrator or by the House of Commons because it was strictly a management right. If the issue could not be settled through negotiations and if it could not be settled through mediation and if a strike could not settle the issue, what other mechanism was left but arbitration to settle the dispute?
In the communication which the owner sent out yesterday, it it was claimed that the issue had been resolved in the past by the Canadian Labour Relations Board and, therefore, there was no reason for it to be settled through arbitration. Again, that is not the truth. As a result of that communication and through the co-operation of the Department's labour officials, I have the previous decisions that were made concerning Prince Rupert. They did not deal with the specific issue which is causing the work stoppage at this time. They dealt with foremen and the position of a supervisor, but they did not deal with the whole category of workers. It is obviously a very important issue in dispute which must be resolved.

I find it unfortunate that there is a management attitude in some parts of the country that if it is dirty work, it is union work, but if it is computer work where you punch buttons, it is management work. There are a lot of highly trained people in the Public Service, engineers, doctors, and other professionals. There are people in the largest companies in this country who have degrees and are members of unions. However, there is an attitude that if you are playing with buttons on a computer, as opposed to working with a shovel, it cannot be a union job. That attitude will never lead to the settlement of a dispute.
Prior to Christmas the union offered to have the outstanding issue of whether the jobs in question should be done by union members or non-union personnel put forward for arbitration. The union was doing a service for the people of Canada and especially the farmers of western Canada.
I know that all things are not all black and white. I know there may be a reason why former Justice Emmett Hall, with all of his qualifications, was unacceptable to the employer, but surely to God they could have suggested appropriate, qualified and experienced people who are as respectable as former Justice Emmett Hall. They did not do that. Hence we have the legislation before us today.
Although we will not support the legislation I am glad to see that many of the more objectionable clauses in the legislation ordering the postal workers back to work have been dropped from this legislation. One of the concerns we had with the postal worker legislation was that the arbitrator was referred to a particular report which management liked and the workers did not like. We were also upset about what we considered to be an unconstitutional clause in that legislation which denied union members the right to run for re-election for up to five years after they contravened the legislation. We believe that that was completely uncalled for. Some of those things are not contained in this legislation, and to that extent we believe it is an improvement.
However, there is a contradiction in that in the postal workers' legislation where the Government liked the conciliation report it referred to this report and said that the arbitrator must look at it. Just a few minutes ago the Minister said that he would not appoint former Justice Emmett Hall because the union suggested him.
I suggest that former Justice Emmett Hall is respected by all Members of this House and by Canadians right across the land for the work he has done in such important areas as medicare and transportation. He has experience with regard to grain transportation, the very issue of this dispute. If we cannot accept him as an independent-minded arbitrator just because the union suggested his name, then we obviously apply a double standard in back-to-work legislation. Something was acceptable to the Post Office, therefore we put it in the legislation. When something is acceptable to the grain handlers and to most Canadians, we do not put it in the legislation. The Minister said that he will not accept that.

Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
I think there are some problems with the legislation, although I believe it is necessary at this time. 1 find it very unfortunate that the two parties did not get together and resolve the dispute, but 1 do believe we could make this legislation better. 1 hope that in the time we have before us today, after we hear from the Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), in whose riding this dispute is occurring, and from others from western Canada who are concerned about the plight of farmers, the Minister will accept some amendments and send a clear message that when someone as respected as former Justice Emmett Flail is named as a possible mediator perhaps we in this House should respect the fact that that person was available, qualified, experienced, and should have been used.

subtopic: PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLING OPERATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to rise this afternoon to speak on this Bill introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux). The Minister of Labour has given Members of the House a very detailed account of a dispute which has gone on for more than four years. The strike by Grain Workers' Union Local 333 has halted the flow of grain at Canada's newest inland terminal, Prince Rupert Grain 2. This facility is owned by Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. and incorporates state of the art computers and equipment. It has just begun to demonstrate its potential in terms of its role in the prairie grain transportation system. 1 believe it would be useful to look more closely at the PRG 2 operations to give us an indication of the significance of this work disruption to the grain economy.
During the recent parliamentary break I took the opportunity to visit all of the RM councils in my constituency which were having their first meeting of the year. I was able to visit 22 of 27 rural municipalities. That covers a pretty sizable chunk of southwestern Saskatchewan which I represent. Each municipality mentioned the Prince Rupert grain situation. They made mention of the fact that the dispute had been building for years because they had no contract and could not imagine why that situation was allowed to exist. It is not a matter of pointing the finger at either union or management. Both have a responsibility which certainly is not being lived up to.
The grain elevator facility at Prince Rupert was constructed to give the West Coast a second outlet for export grain markets. The facility was rated at the time of its construction to have an annual export capability in excess of 3.5 million tonnes. During the 1986-87 crop year exports totalled 4.2 million tonnes. That level of throughput was achieved using a two-shift operation for the first five months in the crop year beginning August 1, 1986, and a three-shift operation for the last seven months ending July 31, 1987. Under certain conditions with maximum throughput PRG 2 has the potential to reach even greater production and to play an even greater role in West Coast exports.
It should be mentioned that one of the outstanding features of the PRG 2 terminal is its ability to clean grain at a very
high rate. According to the description of the facility published by the company, the terminal has the highest throughput of any grain cleaning elevator in the world. Its high performance, which results from state of the art engineering and technology, allows gain to be cleaned about as fast as it is unloaded.
The significance of this cleaning capacity is that it avoids the potential bottleneck in processing grain and contributes to PRG-2 being one of the most efficient grain terminals in the world.
The Prince Rupert terminal is serviced by CN Rail which transports grain through the mountains and connects thousands of grain producers to the terminal. Grain is received on one of the four tracks at the terminal and each of these tracks is capable of accommodating an entire train. The terminal storage bins can hold approximately 210,000 tonnes and shiploading is done at a very high rate through three tower mounted spouts. This gives us an indication of the operation of Prince Rupert Grain No. 2.
What is perhaps most outstanding about PRG2 is the fact that all of the grain-handling functions and grain flows at the plant are remotely controlled and monitored by computer from the elevator grain centre.
As has been described earlier by the Minister of Labour, it is the manning of this computerized grain centre that is one of the key issues in dispute between Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. and the grain workers union.
Earlier I referred to some 4.2 million tonnes of grain exports through PRG2 in the last crop year. This level of export gives the terminal an annual throughput efficiency of approximately 20 times its capacity, compared to perhaps 10 to 13 times capacity at other grain terminals. PRG2's throughput efficiency gives the terminal a very significant role in grain exports. Fourteen per cent of the 1986-87 crop year exports went through Prince Rupert. Prince Rupert's share to December 6, 1987 is unchanged at 14 per cent. In 1986-87, grain exports from the West Coast, that is Prince Rupert and Vancouver combined, amounted to over 16 million tonnes, and PRG2's share of West Coast grain exports amounts to 26 per cent.
It is interesting to note that the facility PRG2 is 80 per cent owned by the prairie co-operatives. It has been mentioned that the Prairie co-operatives also own most of the other ports that load grain into the export market. There has been some suggestion that their position is that the grain will move through their facilities, albeit at another point, and therefore they are not as anxious to settle this particular issue as they might be.
This strike has gone on for more than a month. In fact, it began on December 9 of last year and has been in effect for the better part of five weeks. That is a long time for a terminal
January 19, 1988

to be left idle when our export grain commitments are at an all-time high.
There is no question that responsibility for settling the issue lies with the two parties in dispute. They have demonstrated a complete lack of responsibility, which has resulted in these collective bargaining negotiations breaking down and has caused the present impasse and consequent impact on grain shipments. The parties in dispute have shirked their responsibilities by failing to come to an agreement. Both union and management have a role to play, and it certainly has not been carried out.
The shareholders as well as the union have known for the past four years that this issue must be settled. The manning of the computerized grain centre is in dispute, and this issue must be resolved.
The dispute now poses a severe threat to the prairie grain economy in terms of lost grain sales and in terms of our international reputation as a reliable supplier of grain.
It is indeed a most unfortunate situation. Not only are the grain handlers at this facility out of work, we also hear reports of ships lying idle in the port, waiting to load. As well, there are railway cars to be unloaded at the terminal. Some 80,000 to 90,000 tonnes of grain would normally flow through this terminal in the course of a week. If this situation is allowed to continue, Vancouver elevators would be the only terminal export point available until spring. As Hon. Members are aware, Thunder Bay operates on a reduced scale during the winter. Only a relatively small amount of grain is shipped by rail to the Lower St. Lawrence transfer elevators during the winter months. As long as the Prince Rupert dispute is not resolved, each day will add to the current congestion.
The other problem associated with moving the grain down to the Lower St. Lawrence elevators is the increased cost. That, in addition to the demurrage paid for the ships that are in a position to load, must ultimately be borne by the prairie producers who have no input in this impasse.
This labour dispute points out very clearly that strikes and lock-outs are not the answer. If we must resort to the Government instituting compulsory binding arbitration, as in this particular case, perhaps disputes should never be allowed to get to this stage. Perhaps we have reached the time when we should consider measures such as the Private Members' initiative introduced by the Member for Swift Current- Maple Creek (Mr. Wilson) last summer when we debated this very issue. Perhaps the time has come to consider such a solution.
1 have attempted to describe what I see as the very significant role that this relatively new grain terminal facility plays in the prairie grain economy. PRG2 is a significant new grain export facility, with 26 per cent of West Coast grain exports going through the port. It has the potential to become even more significant in the years ahead.
Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
This work stoppage has brought a halt to the flow of export grain through PRG2 and, in doing so, prevents the realization of the efficiency potential of this important national asset. The company and the union have failed to make the compromises that would resolve their long drawn out dispute, even with the repeated efforts made by the Minister of Labour through conciliation and mediation, including the assistance of Canada's top mediator. The parties have brought their dispute to a critical stage and the Government has no alternative but to require the resumption of operations and the resolution of the issues through arbitration. I urge all Hon. Members to support the Bill and work toward its immediate passage.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to say a few words with respect to the Bill before us today, Bill C-106. I think the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Gustafson) has pointed out the problem. The Government has dillied and dallied around on this matter for too long. It is just getting around to taking action today with respect to this dispute between the grain handlers and the Prince Rupert grain terminal.
The problem has been with us for three or four years and the Government has not really taken any action until earlier this month when it appointed Mr. Kelly as the mediator in this dispute. It became very clear after Mr. Kelly had completed his mediation attempts that only compulsory arbitration, hopefully, joint voluntary compulsory arbitration, could resolve the dispute. That is why the Leader of her Majesty's Official Opposition issued a statement last Friday calling on the Government to call in the parties to propose a suitable arbitrator between the two parties and seek a negotiated settlement thus avoiding this back to work legislation. It seemed clear at that time that if a suitable arbitrator could be found the union involved would go back to work on a voluntary or agreed basis. Unfortunately, after those negotiations last week it appeared obvious that that could not happen. The wheat pools are concerned that an arbitrated settlement may strike at the prerogatives and normal powers of the employer in this case. They see it as a dangerous precedent because the decision that is made with respect to the management role in the operations of this terminal may reduce that role, and some of that management role would be turned over to the union's employees at the terminal.
There seemed to be almost an inevitability that the only solution was compulsory arbitration, as the legislation before us proposes. Clearly, action had to be taken. This morning in the Standing Committee on Agriculture the Commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board suggested that every month the terminal moves $70 million worth of wheat and other grains, and the strike has been going on for over a month. If the terminal is shut down the grain simply does not move. At the other end of the equation, when wheat has to be moved from prairie points to the East Coast ports, there is at least a $15 million loss in additional costs which are not received by the farmers.
We are facing an incredibly difficult time in the grain industry today with prices running at half of what they were five years ago. There is no clear indication that the American Farm Bill will not ratchet down prices another notch or two in this coming year. The Americans are putting up more and more money in the Export Enhancement Program. The budget has been increased to $1.5 billion in direct violation of the
trade agreement that they would not take pre-empted strikes and actions against Canada. The Wheat Board has been selling grain at a maximum rate. We hope the free trade agreement will not have an adverse affect on that body which is doing such a marvellous job in selling our grain and maintaining extremely high quality, which is putting our grain in demand around the world.
The contracts are being put off for delivery from the West Coast by the Canadian Wheat Board now into March or early April because of the strike. There is no question that prairie agriculture is suffering from this strike. We need to take the action which is proposed before the Ffouse today in order to maintain Canada as a reliable supplier and retain its reputation as the best wheat producer and the highest quality wheat producer in the world. We want to see this legislation enacted so that the dispute can be resolved. Perhaps if the Minister had acted last Friday and called in the parties, proposing a series of acceptable arbitrators, we could have had a voluntary agreement and would not have to take the legislative route which is being proposed here today.
We want to study this Bill clause by clause so we can have a more detailed question and discussion kind of format. We believe it is essential that the Port of Prince Rupert be brought back into operation and that grain starts to move on an urgent and immediate basis so that the grain industry, so vital to our entire national economy, can get moving again.

Mr. Speaker, I do not enjoy participating in these kinds of debates involving the ordering of workers back to work. However, it appears that in this situation there were not a lot of options because of the intransigence of the employer. I want to spend a moment on that because I know the Minister crafted his speech to condemn equally Prince Rupert Grain Limited and Local 333. However, there is a larger picture about which Hon. Members should be reminded.
The problem, as Members here know, is that Local 333 has been without a collective agreement for three-and-a-half, going on four years. There are reasons for that. There are reasons for a great many of the delays.
There has been a funny deal in the works ever since 1980 when the federal Government agreed to provide Prince Rupert Grain 1, the old waterfront elevator, to the consortium of Alberta Wheat Pool, Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, United Grain Growers, James Richardson and Sons, Cargill Limited and Manitoba Pool Elevators, an elevator estimated at some $50 million plus in value for $1. The federal Government, as well as the taxpayers of Canada, put in something in excess of $30 million in infrastructure on Ridley Island to Prince Rupert Grain 2, a truly amazing and modern state of the art elevator.
January 19, 1988

People in Prince Rupert do not forget easily, nor do I. Prince Rupert lost some 60 grain jobs as a direct result of the closing of PRO 1 and the opening of PRG 2. There was a direct loss in wages to the Prince Rupert economy of $3 million per year and almost double that if we take into account the lay-offs and movement of CN workers as well as the dislocation of other people in the economy as a result of the direct loss of those very important and longstanding historic jobs in Prince Rupert that have been there for more than half a century.
Just after the last election I asked a question of the then Minister of Transport, the present Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), about the old grain elevator. I knew then, and the same is the case now, that it would long be necessary, as are the jobs, to the Prince Rupert economy. On November 21, 1984, as reported at page 457 of Hansard, he said:
On the issue of the Prince Rupert Grain Terminal, I share the Hon. Member's concern. 1 am deeply disturbed by the prospect of the loss of jobs. I had an opportunity to meet with members of the union during the course of the election campaign, at which time I set out to explore whether there were other ways and means by which the existing terminal could be utilized. There has been some demonstrated interest in that. 1 think there is a way in which that terminal might be used for non-grain services, such as specialty crops, pellets and things of that nature. 1 will be discussing this with some members of the provincial government, and other interested parties, with a view to attempting to maintain that facility, even on a one-shift basis, to help alleviate some of the problems affecting workers. More important, in the long term we should make sure that we do not close down a facility, something which we may regret later on.
That is the signal that the Deputy Prime Minister sent to the grain workers at Prince Rupert. The signal that he sent to Prince Rupert generally is that we are going to keep the old elevator going and get the new elevator under way.
By the time of the opening, farmers were receiving 30 cents more a bushel by using Prince Rupert. Of course, there was a saving to those countries which were sending freighters to pick up grain, a saving of 500 miles each way, particularly for grain vessels from the Orient. Thus Prince Rupert has a great many reasons for being popular, not only with the farmers who receive a better price for their grain by moving it through Prince Rupert. Countries buying grain from Canada receive a better deal because it is even closer than Vancouver.
So there was a change in capacity from 1.2 million tonnes with just PRG 1, which in 1983 was about 15 per cent of West Coast exports, to 3.5 million tonnes, the potential throughput through PRG2, which now, as other Members have pointed out, was 26 per cent of the West Coast exports last year. During the 1983 crop year over 4 million tonnes were shipped through Prince Rupert, providing a very substantial benefit and gain to the farmers of Canada.
I agree with what other Members have said. We have to keep in mind not only the interests of Prince Rupert, the grain workers or anyone else in particular in the local sense of this issue, but the farmers. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), reminded me that
500,000	tonnes were diverted from Prince Rupert to the Lakehead at a $30 per tonne loss to prairie farmers. Once
Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
demurrage, storage and so on is added on to that, one finds that this dispute from December 9 until now has been very costly to the farmers of Canada. There is no doubt that that loss amounts to millions and millions of dollars.
There may have been other measures the Government could have taken. On December 14 the grain workers offered voluntarily to go back to work. They have always wanted to go back to work. Of course, they suggested at that time, and continue to suggest, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall as being an entirely appropriate person to arbitrate such a matter. I agree. 1 think that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) agrees, although he has made some suggestions today that, by the grain workers continuing to suggest Mr. Hall and Prince Rupert Grain Limited not liking the suggestion, that may have made it impossible for him as a Minister to appoint Mr. Hall.
As I stated earlier, the Minister crafted his speech to be equally condemnatory of the union and of Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. I hope he will keep in mind that he should take great care in whom he chooses as an arbitrator. For whatever reasons, the Minister has not included a clause in the Bill requiring the mutual consent of both parties to the appointment of an arbitrator for this very important matter.
Records were set and broken regularly at old Prince Rupert Grain 1 prior to its demolition. It was one hell of a hardworking group that put that all together, with the kind of antiquated equipment it had, particularly in terms of boxcars and in terms of bringing them in, loading them and moving them out very quickly. Some 40 per cent of the union jobs have been lost since 1985. The jobs went from 115 down to 51, while the number of supervisors has grown from 6 to 15. As I pointed out earlier, that is a direct income loss to the Prince Rupert area of $6 million per year in wages alone.
While Prince Rupert Grain 2 has been a welcome facility in terms of high technology and its ability to move a great deal of farmers' grain, it has been a really sore point in Prince Rupert, especially in terms of the promises of more jobs and how great it would be. The great promises from Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. never came to be. In fact, Prince Rupert generally lost, in a net sense, as a result of the new elevator.
As the union pointed out in evidence given to various tribunals and in press releases, it is not opposed to technological change but wants the right to perform the same jobs as are performed by members of the same union in Vancouver. In 1984 the employer would not recognize Local 333's right to continue with its collective agreement to represent employees on Ridley Island. That gives one some idea of the kinds of bad faith that was demonstrated by the employer very early on in the relationship in terms of the development of the Ridley Island site.
The Canada Labour Relations Board upheld the union's right to do so. The employer then laid off 76 employees from Prince Rupert Grain 1. I wish to point out that the Alberta and Saskatchewan Pools have unionized workers operating the computers as panel control operators in Vancouver. They are

January 19, 1988
Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act
the principal owners of Prince Rupert Grain 2. We have to understand the nature of this difficulty. The Minister touched on the matter of manning the grain centres as being the principal problem. He pointed out the discrepancy between what Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. is saying publicly and what the CLRB ruled on. The position being taken by the company is quite different from both the interpretation of the Minister of Labour and what the CLRB ruled in relation to manning the grain centre. It ruled in relation to foremen but never ruled in relation to the level of staffing. There are also the questions of job classification and security to be considered.
The point I want to make is that the same principal owners of Prince Rupert Grain 2 have unionized workers doing these panel jobs in Vancouver, but are making that the key issue blocking a satisfactory settlement through collective bargaining at Prince Rupert.
The employee classification at Prince Rupert Grain 2 has been done by the employer without regard to Prince Rupert Grain Terminal No. 1 in terms of grandfathering, the collective agreement, or the Vancouver operations. I would like to know on the basis of what logic, let alone law, the employer has attempted to stuff that down the throats of Local 333, which, Mr. Speaker, over the last three and a half years has been about as cool-headed a group of bargainers as I have ever seen.
The employer did not respect seniority rights. In fact, many laid off workers were forced to move and find other work while they were waiting for a decision from Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. The employer then contracted out the watchman's work. There has been no agreement since 1983. As the Minister and other Members have pointed out, that is almost four years.
Over the past few weeks the Minister of Labour appointed Bill Kelly to find a solution. The Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) attempted to paint some type of picture that the Opposition have created the delay. We know that the House was sitting on December 14 when the farmers made a proposal, which was then supported by the Grain Workers' Union Local 333, to have arbitration at that point. That was some six weeks ago, so it is hardly appropriate for the government side to be attempting to paint it as some nefarious deal cooked up on the opposition benches.
Of course, the employer refused voluntary arbitration, as Mr. Kelly suggested. Let us not forget that the Minister must exercise care in his choice. I listened with care to his reasons why Mr. Justice Emmett Hall may not now be suitable. Mr. Justice Emmett Hall could in fact end up being the arbitrator in this matter. I listened with care to the reasons of the Minister, and even though it is not in the Bill, I would hope that when looking at his short list the Minister might at least call Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. and Local 333 with a suggested short list to see whether or not mutual consent could not be obtained in that manner.
All along the union has been prepared to accept an agreement negotiated and concluded in June, 1987 in Vancouver. It is the other three contentious issues which, as I have demonstrated could easily have been resolved. Rather than suggesting Mr. Justice Emmett Hall, Henry Kinks of Local 333, could have suggested me. I could have resolved these matters in five minutes, but I am not sure that that would have been entirely appropriate.
I know that farmers across the country are listening to this debate, I know that the grain workers are listening, and I know people in Prince Rupert are listening. But I will speak now for a moment to the farmers. They must ask just who is the employer at Prince Rupert Grain 2 and how well are they being served. How well is the country being served when the grain workers are being treated so shabbily year after year at Prince Rupert? At a time when the U.S. Farm Bill is hurting Canadian farmers, and low prices, high debt, and high costs are all harming Canadians farmers and their families, I think those farmers, particularly those associated with the Alberta Wheat Pool, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, United Grain Growers, James Richardson and Sons, Cargill and Manitoba Pool Elevators should be scratching their heads and wondering how it is possible that a collective agreement and a dispute such as this has to wind its way to Parliament to find resolution.
Farmers may well hold the key. We do not need some type of specialized dispute settlement mechanisms as proposed by the Member from Swift Current. We need some cool heads at Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. and with the cool heads that there have been at Local 333 I think we will find the way out of future disputes, if the farmers take that key. They know what the problem is and they can look at how this dispute has come to be. A similar argument was placed before Committee of the Whole on Bill C-86 in the postal dispute. The Minister as a lawyer is well aware of the arguments put forward at that time, and he is also aware of how justice abhors minimum fines and penalties in any legislation.
I think all Members of the House are aware of the minimum sentence of seven years in jail for importing narcotics. We have had instances of young people caught with a very small amount of marijuana or a drug like that who are subject to a minimum sentence of seven years in jail. It is obviously an abhorrent type of measure. I say that despite the fact that we are talking here about a situation where the employer or the union contravenes the Act and there is a minimum fine of $20,000. In this case, the union is anxious to have binding arbitration while the employer is not and, on a matter of principle, we cannot have in legislation the kind of minimums stated. The judges of this country who deal with offences and contraventions of legislation are very well prepared to deal with them.
I will give one example because I think an example is worthy of note even though it may be theoretical. If we look at Clause 3(b) of the Bill we read:
every employee shall, when so required, forthwith resume the duties of that
employee's employment.
Forthwith, Mr. Chairman, has been interpreted by many courts as to its meaning; namely, that it has to be done right away. If somebody did not report for work right away for some reason, then it may be a very minor period of time, it may be a very minor offence, but it is still subject to a minimum fine. There are also provisions in Clause 4(b) which require a union and each officer or the representative of the union to take all reasonable steps to ensure that employees comply with Clause 3(b).
Some judge might decide that the union or an individual should have done something which the judge thought was reasonable but they did not, and that union or that individual
could be found guilty under this Bill. It may have been a minor or a technical breach, yet a minimum fine would apply.
The Minister of Justice has left the Chamber, so I would like to ask the Minister of Labour to respond to this point. It is a very serious precedent not only to have a minimum penalty in this legislation but in other legislation and I ask him to reconsider the inclusion in a Bill of this type of minimum penalty. There are ways of making sure that the seriousness of the offence is recognized by the judiciary by placing maximum fines or providing for other penalties other than fines. Having a minimum fine in place is not an appropriate measure in dealing with this type of thing.
We have many examples across the country of labour disputes where court orders are issued and sometimes individuals are brought before the court for contempt. In those situations judges deal with the contempt of court order, if there is one in place. This is a similar kind of matter where there is an order from Parliament to return to work. Without any minimum fines or minimum approach, judges across the country are well able to deal with the seriousness of crimes committed in similar circumstances. Sometimes jail penalties are provided and sometimes very large fines, sometimes fines as large as those proposed here are imposed.
Could the Minister of Labour tell the House why it is that he is including this type of minimum fine in the Bill when there is an opportunity to accomplish the same object without this measure?

Canada-Alaska Boundary Act
Members of the House will know that just over a year ago the legislative committee chose this as one of the Bills to be brought before the House for a vote. Through a variety of calendar changes ranging from the changing of opposition days and government days to the proroguing of the House, Bill C-222 did not get to the floor of the House for a vote. I am hoping that before 20 minutes after six this evening Members of the House will allow this Bill to come to a vote so that it can either go to committee or be passed into law.
Everyone who has followed the rather sad history of the disputes in relation to 54-40 will know how important it is that a statutory and parliamentary vote be taken putting the A-B line into law, not to send a message to individual Canadians but to send a collective message to Washington that we are tired of the steps they have taken throughout this century to try to capture a part of Canada which has always been Canada and is supported by many treaties.
I would like to thank my colleague, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), who spoke on this Bill the last time around. I hope that the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) and others will take the opportunity to participate in this debate today because 1 think it is an historic moment for this House to pass Bill C-222 into law. it entrenches the boundary lines from Cape Muzon to Cape Chacon, to the opening of the Portland Canal.
Let me outline the location of that boundary. The Alaskan Panhandle which comes down the north coast of British Columbia and ends just above the Queen Charlotte Islands where an area known as Dixon Entrance Lies. Prince Rupert lies in that immediate vicinity and there is extensive fishing in Dixon Entrance.
The history of the A-B line essentially begins in 1825 with a treaty that was struck between Russia and Great Britain. At that time, and well into the century, Britain produced our treaties for Canada. That was followed by another treaty in 1867, after what was probably the greatest land transaction in the history of the world when the United States purchased Alaska from Imperial Russia for $15 million in gold. Just as in 1825, the 1867 treaty included very specific references to 5440 as being the southern terminus of the territory that was acquired from Imperial Russia.
There was some trouble in that area during the gold rush period in 1897 and 1898, up the Stikine, through various of the transboundary rivers and over the Chilcoot.
As well, President McKinley was assassinated in 1901 and was succeeded by President Teddy Roosevelt. He was a rather notorious and rowdy President, who did not like the trouble among the miners in the disputed area between Alaska, British Columbia and the Yukon. He threatened then Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier with sending troops into the area north of Prince Rupert and up into the transboundary areas to quell this so-called uprising.
Not many who have studied history will forget the cry of "54-40" by the Americans back in 1884. That became a famous slogan of the United States that wanted to move the boundary from Oregon all the way up to join the southern terminus of Soviet territory at that time, 54-40 and further up so that the United States would effectively have been all of North America.
The events in 1903 were unfortunate in relation to the rest of the Alaskan Panhandle. However, it supports very strongly my Bill because the Hay-Herbert Treaty was brought forward. Teddy Roosevelt wanted to ensure that there were no Canadian MP's who did not understand how serious he was. He appointed his Secretary of War, E. Root, the Secretary of State, Henry Cabot Lodge and George Turner, the senior Republican senator from the State of Washington.
As 1 stated earlier, at that time Great Britain was responsible for making our treaties and therefore sent Lord Alberton from the House of Lords. We also had on our side the Lieutenant Governor of the Province of Quebec and a lawyer from Toronto. That was the Canadian contingent, up against the Secretary of War, the Secretary of State and the senior Republican senator from the northwestern United States.
Unfortunately, Lord Alberton voted with the three Americans on six of the seven boundary questions and gave up about
10,000	square miles of Canada to the United States. This included all of the headwaters and the beautiful inlets up the north coast of British Columbia which were never part of the 1867 treaty or 1825 treaty. These were given to the United States, effectively closing off the northern half of British Columbia from access to ice-free ports, of which Stewart is the most northerly ice-free port on the West Coast of North America.
There was a four to two vote on the six questions of the Panhandle, but a unanimous vote on the A-B line, 54-40. It was unanimously ratified, placed into the Hay-Herbert Treaty, an international treaty, passed through all of its necessary legislative means in the United States, which entrenched the A-B line as the international boundary.
Finally, in 1909, six years after the Americans had taken charge of a big chunk of Canada, an Order in Council finally wove its way through the august chambers here when Cabinet met and said it should do something about the A-B line. By 1911, Canadians not only in British Columbia but right across the country were still enraged about the 1903 rip-off. The newspapers from 1903 to 1911 will show that Canadians continued to be angry, whether in Toronto, Moose Jaw, Prince Rupert or elsewhere. People everywhere felt very badly about how we were treated.
It is interesting how history collides with itself from time to time. At that time the Government of Canada had initiated free trade talks with the United States. It was the dispute over the A-B line that brought about a quick end to those talks. The people of Canada rejected the free trade talks with the United States in 1911.

For many years the A-B line disappeared into the mists of time until a conscious decision appears to have been taken in Washington by the State Department to start harassing Canadians, almost simultaneously with the kind of boundary harassment we saw on George's Bank and have now come to see on a more regular basis in the Beaufort in relation to the 141st meridian between Alaska and Yukon.
In June, in 1981, a vessel known as Sable Mist was boarded. This caused a great furor on the north coast of British Columbia and protests by fishermen who closed off the Port of Prince Rupert, ferry traffic movements and so on.
In July, 1981, a number of American vessels attempted to come to fish in Canadian waters south of 54-40. Those six fishing vessels were ordered back out of Dixon Entrance.
In May, 1984, the Secretary of the Interior of the United States offered 40 square miles of Canada off the Queen Charlotte Islands for sale. That did not attract too much attention for some days and, in fact, the Federal Register, Volume 49, No. 63, published March 30, 1984, offered this particular sale of a chunk of Canada by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior to various U.S. oil and gas companies.
I raised that matter in the House and the Minister promised and subsequently sent a note of protest to Washington. In the next publication of the Federal Register, the sale was withdrawn.
The Learmonth Bank, the area in the Dixon Entrance above which many anadromous and non-anadromous species tend to school, has long been of interest to both Canadian and American fishermen. It was in relation to the Learmonth Bank in 1984 that the Storus and Brooks Bay were boarded inside Canadian territory by the U.S. navy and coast guard. Again, notes were sent by Canada to Washington.
The issue became more involved when President Reagan and Secretary of State George Shultz became more interested in the A-B line. There were a number of reasons for this.
There was enormous fishing value, enormous gas and oil potential. Polymetallic sulphides have already been located on the ocean floor. There are military reasons as well. The Americans want to move various Trident submarine related activities into the southern Panhandle area. This has raised jurisdictional questions and so on.
There is a very serious test of Canada's will and our ability to stand together on an issue which exists even today.
It was just two years ago that George Shultz appointed Ed Derwinski as the U.S. negotiator for the A-B line. He is a 25-year member of Congress and someone we know through the Canada-U.S. group and other meetings. He is a very knowledgeable and respected member of the U.S. House.

One can only wonder what kind of advice he was receiving from various bureaucrats and officials at the Department of External Affairs to have even considered entering into negotiations on the A-B line. It has always been Canada's boundary. Why would any government want to get involved in negotiations? If would be the same as if some bum walked in off the street into your home, Mr. Speaker, and said: "I would like to negotiate this house. Why do you not get out?" What was being proposed out of the Department of External Affairs was that someone could come in and say: "This house is actually mine. Let us negotiate a price. How about $50?" Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think I am quite familiar with Bill C-22. I am quite aware that this is Bill C-222. I am sure it will not provide a headache, hopefully, for the Hon. Member or anyone else in this House.
Indeed, there is no doubt that the A-B line was indeed established by the 1903 Alaska boundary award and that it divides the lands of Alaska and Canada. That is the view of both Canada and the United States. But the United States insists that it is the land boundary only in the sense of a line for the allocation of the land territories alone and not for the allocation of sea areas under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of either country. Canada, on the other hand, has always taken the position that the A-B line is not only a boundary dividing the land but a maritime boundary as well, and that the waters south of that line are Canadian, together with the sea bed under them.
January 19, 1988

Regrettably, Bill C-222 would seem to adopt something like the U.S. view of this matter instead of the Canadian view. The language of the Bill, given the history of this dispute, requires greater precision if it is to avoid being interpreted in that way.
I think that there are problems with the drafting of the Bill. One might say that that can be fixed up when and if it goes to committee, if they deal merely with technical areas. However, these problems are also symptomatic of different difficulties that could arise if we ignore the language of Bill C-222 and address its apparent intention instead.
Imagine for a moment that the Bill before us did enshrine in a clear statutory form the longstanding Canadian position with regard to the A-B line in Dixon Entrance. We would still have to ask ourselves whether such a Bill would truly achieve its objectives, or whether it might harm the very interests it seeks to protect. These objectives and interests would be to secure Canada's maritime sovereignty in the Dixon Entrance beyond all doubt of challenge. But could any Bill do this?
The answer is clear. No domestic law or other unilateral action can of itself resolve a boundary dispute with another sovereign state. International law and practice lay down a few basic guidelines for the settlement of maritime boundary disputes between neighbouring countries. I think, as my colleague will recall, these were well stated by the Chamber of the International Court of Justice in its 1984 decision in the Gulf of Maine case. I quote:
No maritime delimitation between states with opposite or adjacent coasts may be effected unilaterally by one of those states. Such delimination must be sought and effected by means of an agreement, following negotiations conducted in good faith and with the genuine intention of achieving a positive result. Where, however, such agreement cannot be achieved, delimitation should be effected by recourse to a third party possessing the necessary competence.
Of course, it can be said that the A-B line in Dixon Entrance is itself the result of a third party settlement by the Alaska Boundary Tribunal. That, indeed, is Canada's position regarding the status of the A-B line as a maritime boundary. The United States, however, does not accept that position. Successive Canadian Governments have recognized that the only way forward in this matter is either by negotiation or by international adjudication. So far, negotiation has been the preferred route, although it has not yet brought about the result that we in Canada would like to see.
Any Bill enshrining the A-B line as a maritime boundary in Canadian law might well rule out the possibility of a negotiated settlement and virtually force Canada to refer the dispute to third party proceedings. Is that what the Hon. Member for Skeena wants? Is that what the House wants? International adjudication is a valuable last resort, but one to be entered into by design rather than by mere accident.
Hon. Members will be aware that discussions on the West Coast boundaries were suspended in 1979, pending the conclusion of the Gulf of Maine case. With that case behind
Canada-Alaska Boundary Act
us, the U.S. Secretary of State, George Shultz, suggested that special representatives be appointed to oversee discussions and possible negotiations on West Coast maritime boundaries.
Before responding to Mr. Shultz, the Secretary of State for External Affairs sought the views of the Government of British Columbia. He also heard from numerous groups and communities on the West Coast. Having carefully weighed their views and the attitude of the provincial Government, he concluded that now is not an opportune time for Canada to resume discussions with the United States on West Coast maritime boundary matters. In reaching this conclusion the Minister was conscious of the sensitivity of the issues involved, particularly with respect to Dixon Entrance, and the need to allow some breathing space to ensure the smooth implementation of the Canada-U.S.A. Pacific Salmon Treaty.
At the same time, however, the Secretary of State advised Mr. Shultz that he intends to keep the situation under review and to leave open the possibility of taking up his proposal for discussions on the boundary at some future time when circumstances may be more propitious.
Whether we negotiate now or later, or whether it is ultimately decided to refer the question to third party settlement, we must still ask ourselves whether any version of Bill C-222 might advance the Canadian position. I have already indicated that domestic legislation would not resolve the problem under international law. But could it have some effect on the United States? Let me ask the question another way.
How would Canada react if the U.S. Congress were to adopt a law of its own regarding the maritime boundary in Dixon Entrance? Such a law, we can be sure, would incorporate an equidistant line dividing Dixon Entrance equally between Canada and the United States. That, of course, is the U.S. position regarding the maritime boundary in Dixon Entrance. So far, the United States has only declared its position in a public notice in the U.S. Federal Register, and has done so on the express condition that such notice be without prejudice to any negotiations with Canada.
A law adopted by Congress in response to some variation on Bill C-222 might not include a condition of this kind, as Bill C-222 does not. No doubt Canada would protest a unilateral attempt by the United States, France, or Denmark, to settle a disputed boundary by domestic legislation. But what credibility would our protest carry if we ourselves had acted in the same way?
There is no way in which any version of Bill C-222 can help to resolve the dispute with the United States over the maritime boundary in Dixon Entrance. Any such legislation would only aggravate the dispute. It would induce a more forthcoming attitude by the United States. Indeed, it would virtually guarantee the opposite result and place us in a situation from which we could probably only extricate ourselves by international adjudication.

January 19, 1988

The Hon. Member for Skeena might well respond that Canada cannot be forced into third party proceedings against its will. Strictly speaking he would be right, since the United States and Canada are under no binding reciprocal obligation to refer their disputes to an adjudication. But if we reject negotiation and refuse adjudication, the result is an impasse, something like the situation we were in earlier today with the Prince Rupert grain situation. An impasse could lead to incidents. Incidents can lead all to easily to confrontation. Each side scrambles to stake out its claim at the expense of the other. 1 need hardly spell out the implication of such a development in the Dixon Entrance area.
Clearly, there must be a way to deal with this issue which is mutually satisfactory to both sides. To be sure, there have been incidents from time to time, but thanks to a policy of mutual restraint these have been isolated and have remained manageable.
Any version of Bill C-222 would put this delicate equilibrium at risk, with unpredictable implications for fishing patterns and offshore resource exploration in the disputed area. The impact on the halibut fishery could prejudice local interests. And what about the implications for the Pacific Salmon Treaty? Surely, the last thing we should contemplate at this stage is to say or do anything that might interfere with the successful implementation of the salmon treaty.
We have other outstanding maritime boundary questions to resolve with the United States. They include those seaward of Dixon Entrance, those seaward of Juan de Fuca Straits, in the Beaufort Sea, and both landward and seaward of the boundary fixed by the International Court of Justice in the Gulf of Maine area. In addition, we have boundaries to settle with Denmark in the Lincoln Sea and with France off the coasts of Newfoundland and St. Pierre and Miquelon.
I have only spoken of the possible implications of Bill C-222 for Dixon Entrance. I do not wish to address its possible implications for other areas in question in the limited time I have. Let me only say that I doubt whether they have been given adequate thought in the preparation of the Bill before us today.
We do not need legislation to protect Canada's position in Dixon Entrance. We do not need it to convince ourselves of the rightness of Canada's position there. We do not need it to convince the United States of our own convictions. Finally, we do not need it for the greater certainty that Bill C-222 promises but does not truly deliver.

fishing vessel that United States vessels were not permitted to fish anywhere in Hecate Strait or in any other territorial waters off the coast of British Columbia. Although this Canadian assertion of jurisdiction was protested by the United States, it constitutes early evidence of a Canadian claim to the waters of Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance.
In the 1890s the growth of activity in the area made the need for a definitive settlement of the entire boundary between Canada and Alaska more pressing. The matter was discussed throughout the decade by the Canadian and British Governments on the one side and the United States Government on the other. In 1892 a convention was signed providing for a joint survey of the territory adjacent to the boundary, but the task was not successfully completed. By the beginning of this century, the views of the Governments concerned were irreconcilable, negotiation had failed to settle the dispute, and arbitration seemed the only solution. In 1903 Great Britain and the United States agreed to refer the interpretation of the 1825 treaty to arbitration.
The arbitration treaty of 1903 put three questions to the arbitral tribunal, the answers to which would give an authoritative interpretation of the relevant article of the 1825 treaty. Those questions were as follows: first, what is the intended point of commencement of the line; second, what channel is the Portland Channel; and, third, what course should the line take from the point of commencement to the entrance to Portland Channel?
The first and third of these questions are obviously the most relevant to the subject under discussion, and the third question is of particular interest.
The arbitral tribunal was able to reach quick agreement on the first question before it. The point of commencement was Cape Muzon on Dali Island and not Cape Chacon, the southernmost point on Prince of Wales Island.
The second question-which channel is Portland Channel- gave rise to one of the key controversies in the whole case. In deciding the issue, the tribunal opted partially for the British view, drawing the line north of Pearse and Wales Islands but then through Tongass Channel to run south of Sitklan and Kannaghunut Islands.
The third question was also the subject of some dispute. Great Britain argued that the line should be a straight line drawn from Cape Muzon to the Portland Channel provided that if that line intersected Prince of Wales Island, the whole island would, in accordance with the 1825 treaty, still belong to the United States. The United States contended that the line should run along latitude 54 degrees 40' N. In the end the tribunal accepted the British argument and drew a straight line from Cape Muzon to the entrance to Portland Channel. This is the line that has become known as the A-B Line.
The 1903 Alaska Boundary Award gave rise to a storm of protest in Canada. The complaints concerned the location of the boundary on the mainland, and particularly the division of
the four islands at the entrance to Portland Channel. Much of the Canadian outrage was directed at the British jurist, Lord Alverstone, who was suspected of selling out to the Americans.
In spite of this hostile reaction, the line drawn by the tribunal, which established the contour of the Alaska panhandle, was accepted as definitive by both Canada and the United States so far as it concerned the land, but a dispute ultimately arose with respect to the waters.
Following the 1903 award, Canada continued to assert exclusive fishing rights in the waters of Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance. I have already mentioned an incident in 1897 when Canada issued a warning to an American vessel found fishing in Hecate Strait. A similar incident occurred in 1905 and, as on the previous occasion, the United States protested the Canadian action.
In 1909 the State Department received further complaints from United States fishermen and, as a result, the Secretary of State wrote to the British Ambassador at Washington to request an official statement on the British position with respect to the waters of Hecate Strait. This led to the adoption in 1909 of an Order in Council asserting Canadian jurisdiction over both Hecate Strait and the waters of Dixon Entrance south of the A-B Line. This same position was maintained in another Order in Council in 1914.
In 1910, however, the United States officially asserted its position that the waters of Hecate Strait and Dixon Entrance beyond the three-mile limit were not British waters.
Since World War I, various incidents have occurred that tend to support Canada's position regarding the status of the A-B line. For example, in 1924 a United States cruiser seized a Canadian fishing vessel in Clarence Strait seven and one-half miles north of the A-B line and five miles from the nearest United States shore. The United States reportedly justified this seizure on the ground that the vessel was fishing well north of the international boundary. This incident would appear to suggest that the United States considered the A-B Line to be a boundary for both land and sea.
It is also worth noting that at least until 1921 the International Boundary Commissioners concerned with fixing the Alaska boundary did not treat the A-B line differently from other sections of the Alaska boundary. In particular, during the 1920s the American Commissioner tried to persuade his Canadian counterpart to agree to request their Governments to move the boundary line from Cape Muzon to the middle of the Dixon Entrance, because its position at Cape Muzon was anomalous, as it meant that there was no United States territorial sea off Cape Muzon.
In the 1940s there were unsuccessful attempts to settle the issue by negotiation. Efforts to negotiate a settlement were made again in the 1970s, but these efforts too did not succeed.
Throughout the years from the 1890s to the present Canada has maintained that the waters of Dixon Entrance are Canadian, and Canadian practice since that time has been
January 19, 1988

consistent with that position. In this regard several more recent Canadian measures are particularly noteworthy. For example, in 1964, when the fishing activities of Russian and Japanese vessels off Canada's West Coast began to increase, the Canadian Government issued a warning for them to stay out of the Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait. Both Governments heeded the warning and, apart from a few minor incursions, their fishing vessels have not entered these waters.
In addition, in 1971, under the authority of the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act, Canada delimited its exclusive fisheries jurisdiction within Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait by means of the A-B line and a line drawn across the Dixon Entrance from Cape Muzon to Langara Island. This action by Canada was protested by the United States. Nevertheless, Canada's position on the status of Dixon Entrance and Hecate Strait has remained unchanged.
I opened my remarks today with a reference to the long and colourful history of the Dixon Entrance question. All Members of the House will agree that this brief account of that history and of state practice in the area generally supports the view that the A-B line is the boundary for both land and water inside Dixon Entrance. That is Canada's longstanding view, and it is this view that Canada can and must affirm in any negotiations with the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I should first like to express appreciation to the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) who has just done much to clarify the disputed area, if I can use that word. As was pointed out by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), it is a pity that we cannot have large maps here so that everyone can see the different parts of which we are speaking. However, I think the speech just delivered is the best one can do without a map.
I notice that several of our colleagues from British Columbia are participating in the debate tonight. It is nice to hear correct pronunciation of all these places, which is rather startling, as we who come from Esquimalt-Saanich and such places know. However, tonight there has been a welcome absence of those mistakes.
In discussing the question of the Dixon Entrance, it is important to remember that boundary delimitations are more than a matter of law and that they may have a significant impact on the allocation of resources, both living and nonliving. In the brief time allowed to me I should like to focus on the natural resource potential of the area surrounding Dixon Entrance.
First it should be noted that the subsurface geology of Dixon Entrance has not been studied extensively, but certain inshore tests, seismic profiles, and extrapolations based on wells drilled in Hecate Strait and on Graham Island have offered some clues to assist us in estimating the prospects of oil and gas in and around the area in dispute. The results of these analyses indicate, for example, that the volcanic and sedimentary rocks
Canada-Alaska Boundary Act
under Dixon Entrance may be sufficiently thick and deep to permit the generation and entrapment of certain hydrocarbons. In general, though, the over-all oil and gas potential in the area is believed to be modest at best.
In the time I spent in Prince Rupert many years ago, it was entirely a fishing town. I see that the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) is shaking his head. I was there long before he was born and spent considerable time in Prince Rupert. Of course, some people say that in Prince Rupert a short time seems like a long time, but I enjoyed the hospitality of the people of Prince Rupert and of the civic Government there.
In those days, the city was practically overrun with Americans. There were more American troops there than there were Canadian plus the local inhabitants, but everyone got along very well. We certainly had sufficient fish resources, shrimps, crabs and the like to instil a lifelong love of seafood in anyone who spent any time in Prince Rupert.
The frequency of exploration activity in the area is modest. The first federal permits for oil and gas in Dixon Entrance were acquired in August of 1961 by Husky Oil, a Calgary and Edmonton corporation. Following a perfunctory seismic exploration program, these lands were subsequently surrendered. In December, 1964, Pan American, which is now Amoco Canada Petroleum, Filed on permits North and West of Graham Island including the area of Dixon Entrance North to the A-B line.
At the same time, outside the Entrance, permits were taken up to an equidistant line, with a caveat placed on those submerged land areas impinging directly on the line. Seismic exploration and onshore geological surveys were also undertaken in the area in 1966. Successes, however, were few and far between, as evidenced by the fact that the permits in and outside the Entrance were surrendered in December, 1967.
South of Dixon Entrance in Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound and within the Queen Charlotte tertiary basin, Shell Canada acquired exploration permits for about 3.5 million hectares. The company conducted geological mapping and offshore seismic surveys and drilled exploratory wells in the period from 1967 to 1969, with generally negative results.
In 1970, Shell entered into a farm-out agreement with Chevron Canada Resources whereby Chevron would earn an interest in the Shell offshore area by conducting seismic surveys and by drilling two deep exploratory wells. Some of the wells I invest in are too deep, that is, t-o-o, so much a foot.
Currently, submerged lands held by the petroleum industry for exploration purposes include two blocks held by Petro-Canada Resources Ltd. in Dixon Entrance, a small block by Union Oil Company of Canada located immediately northeast of Graham Island and the northern end of a large block of Hecate Strait held by Shell Canada Resources and operated

by Chevron Canada Resources under the terms of the farm-out agreement to which I have already referred.
The United States has also indicated some tentative interest in the oil and gas potential of the area. Indeed, in 1984, the United States took the first steps toward calling for bids for offshore leases that would have included an area claimed by Canada outside Dixon Entrance. This action prompted a Canadian protest. Subsequently, Canada was informed by the United States that the proposed offers of lease sales had been withdrawn due to lack of interest by the petroleum industry.
Notwithstanding Canadian holdings and some United States interest in the area, little new has been learned about the resources base in the area since the late 1960s. This is due in large part to a moratorium on exploration and oil tanker traffic in the area which was imposed in 1972 by our federal Government.
The 1972 moratorium was intended to prevent crude oil tankers travelling through Dixon Entrance, Hecate Strait and Queen Charlotte Sound en route from the Trans-Alaska pipeline terminal at Valdez, Alaska. Subsequently, a federal Order in Council indefinitely relieved existing offshore exploration permit holders from their obligations to conduct exploratory drilling in these waters and prohibited any further drilling.
In 1981 the Province of British Columbia declared the area an inland marine zone. At the same time, an indefinite moratorium was placed on offshore exploration in Johnston Strait South of Telegraph Cove and in the Straits of Georgia and Juan de Fuca. These respective moratoria are still in effect.
In June, 1984 the federal and British Columbia Ministers of the Environment appointed a five-member environmental assessment panel to conduct a public review of the environmental and related socio-economic effects of any renewed program of petroleum exploration off the West Coast of Canada North of Vancouver Island.
At that time, consideration was being given to lifting the moratorium so that exploration programs could be pursued. Accordingly, the West Coast offshore exploration environmental assessment panel was asked to develop recommendations on the terms and conditions under which petroleum exploration could proceed in a safe and environmentally responsible manner.
During the course of the review, the panel gathered information on the environmental and related socio-economic effects of the proposed offshore exploration program and held two series of public forums in November, 1984 and in the latter part of 1985.
Chevron Canada Resources and Petro-Canada were designated by the federal and provincial regulatory bodies as proponents of the offshore oil and gas exploration activity. As proponents, they were expected to develop information on environmental and socio-economic effects that might result
from exploration activity in their area of interest and to explain and answer questions related to this information during the public hearings. In November 1984, Petro-Canada withdrew from the review process, explaining that it had other higher priorities.
During the course of the environmental assessment panel's review which is now completed, participants raised a variety of concerns, the most serious of which related to the biophysical and socio-economic impacts associated with the level of risk and the potential for a major oil well blowout. Other significant concerns and issues raised included the social and cultural impacts on the area's residents, the biophysical effects associated with seismic surveying and routine exploratory drilling and compensation programs for losses and damages which might result from a major oil well blowout.

Mr. Speaker, have you ever had the opportunity to visit the Eaton Centre-not the West Edmonton Mall-I am referring to the Eaton Centre in Toronto? I can see by the smile on your face that you have been there and you have visited many of the delightful shops and wonderful stores. I know you are aware that the Eaton Centre in Toronto is a people place. It is filled with fountains, trees, walkways, and hundreds and hundreds of people mill about. I bet you did not know that originally when the Eaton
January 19, 1988

Centre was built people thought it would be a gigantic flop. It does a booming business, but it does a booming business in more than one way, that of runaway teenagers.
The police in Metropolitan Toronto and the social service agencies indicate that if there is one place in Metropolitan Toronto area that runaways tend to concentrate and head for it is the Eaton Centre. There at the Eaton Centre they are met by all sorts of weird people. They are met by drug users, drug pushers and pimps. These people offer runaway teenagers a helping hand. They befriend them. They offer them help and a place to stay. Sometimes that place to stay may only be an abandoned house or an abandoned hotel, but they give them the guiding hand. In addition to that they offer them other things, like drugs. Pretty soon after they have taken the opportunity of utilizing all the things being offered by these "wonderful" people, they are into all sorts of things themselves. They are into drugs, drug trafficking, breaking and entering, muggings, street soliciting and prostitution.
There have been a number of cases of individuals of this sort reported in our own press in Toronto, one of them the Kristy McFarlane situation, a 17-year old girl who was found dead of a heroin overdose in a stairwell of a hotel. Another case which has been reported very recently and extensively in the press is that of Kelly Anne Mombourquette, a 14-year old runaway who lived in stairwells, walked the streets and recently, at the preliminary hearing of three people charged with her murder, there was a report that she had died a very, very violent death.
We would like to think these are very isolated cases, but they are not. There are many other cases of runaway teenagers. There have been cases that I am aware of in my own constituency and I suspect there are cases of which you are aware as well. You and I, Mr. Speaker, I, anyway, and I am sure, the Parliamentary Secretary saw the television documentary program back in September entitled Runaways. That program indicated quite clearly that this is not a phenomenon unique to Metropolitan Toronto. It is something that occurs in all parts of Canada, whether it be Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Alberta or British Columbia. Runaways was a shocking program to me in many aspects, but particularly the last scenes. You will recall in the last scene where you and I, the viewers, came face to face with a teenage runaway who was engaged in the process of taking a syringe and shooting up with heroin or with some other drug, sitting there talking to us just a few feet in front of us on our television screens. If nothing else shocked us. that certainly did. It certainly shocked me.
What can we do as a Government and a country to help runaways and their families like this? The Government has already taken a number of initiatives one of which is a pilot program to deal with runaway victims of child abuse. The Government recently announced a drug program which involves a health aspect and more criminal legislation to seize the profits and proceeds from this sort of crime. Of course there is tighter enforcement. Prostitution is another aspect of the problem. We have had new legislation passed within the
Adjournment Debate
last few months dealing with street solicitation and prostitution. Then there is child pornography, and before the House right now is Bill C-54 which deals in an important way with that dreadful problem. Missing children is another aspect, and again recently the Government has undertaken a program to deal with missing children.
You and I and the Parliamentary Secretary, Mr. Speaker, know very well that there are other things we should be doing, many other things. Things have been suggested such as the use of street workers, and the Children's Aid in Metropolitan Toronto is doing that sort of a thing now. The suggestion has been made of support groups to support the parents and the teenagers to try to get them back together again. The mother of Kristy McFarlane suggested that we need more protection for witnesses to testify against the people who lure the runaways into these illegal activities. We need more shelters for runaway teenagers. We need more programs on child abuse. Quite frankly, we need something to enable the police to deal with the situation, not just when teenagers who have run away are considered to be at substantial risk.
There are many things that we should be doing, and it only takes political will on the part of the Government. Tonight I expect the Parliamentary Secretary to stand up in his place and tell us that the Government has that firm political will. I hope he will spell out in detail specific steps which the Government intends to take to deal with this dreadful problem in Canadian society, the problem of runaway teenagers on our streets.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
