speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 10, 1987, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) asked a question on the subject of runaway youth and the CBC television special Runaways, the problem of street children and youth. I wish to take a few minutes to tell Members about some of our Government's initiatives directed at the problem of runaways and to place these initiatives within the context of concerted action on the broader matter of family violence.
The television special vividly introduced many of us to a problem which is representative of a set of related problems experienced by many Canadian families. These include child sexual abuse, spousal assault, drug abuse, child prostitution and pornography and abducted children. Together these problems challenge the response capacities of our social service, health, police and court systems. This Government is committed to addressing these problems and has been deliberate in formulating action.
Bill C-15 on child sexual abuse became law on January 1, 1988, and Bill C-54 on pornography was introduced on May 4, 1987. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police have established a national missing children's registry. The Department of Justice has collaborated with provinces in establishing a tracing service. Within their various mandates, we have mobilized the Departments of Justice, National Health and Welfare and Indian Affairs and Northern Development; the Ministries of

January 19, 1988
Adjournment Debate
the Solicitor General, the Secretary of State and the Status of Women and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to plan collaboratively comprehensive action on the prevention of family violence. The breadth of involvement of government Departments serves to demonstrate the various and many factors which must be considered in responding to these pervasive problems.
While the federal Government may take limited, unilateral action on family violence, it must be recognized that provincial and territorial Governments constitutionally provide front-line services. As well the voluntary sector has long been a source of family support.
Our success in preventing and treating these problems will only result through collaboration with provinces, territories and voluntary groups. In recognition of this fact, a special adviser on child sexual abuse was appointed on August 25, 1987, and has initiated consultations aimed at a national strategy on this problem. Further, officials of National Health and Welfare and other Departments are planning to begin consultations with provincial and territorial Governments on all aspects of family violence.
The problems introduced by the TV program Runaways are complex in their origins and in their solutions. Regardless, all in this House would agree that we must give our every effort to their treatment and prevention. I believe that these few comments indicate to Members that we are making that effort.
CANADIANS OVER AMERICAN INVESTMENT-REQUEST FOR DETAILS/CONTROL OVER AMERICAN INVESTMENT

Mr. Speaker, this adjournment debate relates to an exchange I had with the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) on October 7.
I was dissatisfied with the response I received from her at that time. My question was asked in an attempt to point out to the Hon. Minister the fact that more than 99 per cent of the new jobs that had been created in Canada between 1978 and 1985 had in fact come from Canadian controlled companies, that American-controlled companies had made next to no contribution to job creation in this country and yet Canada was abandoning any effective means of trying to get better performance from foreign-owned companies, particularly American, because of the trade agreement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) signed with the President.
I am always impressed by the ability of the Minister for International Trade to believe anything she likes so long as she tries hard enough. That is certainly the case in this particular instance. I suggested that under the agreement Canadians would not be allowed to say anything at all about American investments. She said that she did not understand the NDP's what she called "obsession" with American firms. She said:
The American firms that we are talking about will still be subject to
monitoring by Investment Canada.
I have taken the trouble to look at the agreement, Mr. Speaker. As you well know, the current limit on Investment Canada reviews is of takeovers and investment of over $5 million. According to the agreement, that will be raised to $25 million in respect to American firms taking over Canadian ones after 1989, to $50 million after 1990, to $100 million in 1991, and to $150 million in 1992 and thereafter. In other words, there will be a 30-fold increase. That effectively means that almost all takeovers by American firms of Canadian firms will not be subject to review. Therefore, the Minister's statement that Investment Canada will continue to subject these American firms to monitoring is just plainly not true.
The Minister said:
We insist that we have sold out nothing.
However, if you look at the elements of the agreement with respect to investment, they indicate that the parties are not to impose export, local content, local sourcing, or import substitution requirements on each other's investors. Effectively the Government of Canada, acting for the people of Canada, will no longer have the ability to try to insist that foreign-controlled companies coming from the United States which are active in Canada act on behalf of Canada or to implement a Canadian industrial strategy. The Minister said that we have given away nothing. In fact, we have given away our power to have an industrial strategy insofar as it affects foreign-controlled companies with parent companies in the United States.
The Minister then said:
We have protected our right to invest in America.
That was never in question, Mr. Speaker. The statement by the United States that they will give national treatment to Canadian firms investing in the United States is all very well, but there have never been particular problems at that level. When Dominion Textile recently tried to take over Burlington Industries, we saw that there are problems at the state and local levels in the United States. National treatment does not get you freedom from state and local interference in Canadian takeovers or investment in the United States.
It is ironical that the Americans, who have such a large control of their own economy, jump up and scream when Canadian firms go from 5 per cent to 7 per cent control of a particular industry, whereas we have tolerated 50 per cent or more control in many of our industries.
The Minister then said that the Government welcomes foreign investment because foreign investment creates jobs. She rejects utterly the evidence from Statistics Canada which I sought to cite in the House of Commons which is absolutely compelling. That evidence indicates that over the course of time from 1978 to 1985 Canadian-controlled companies created 876,400 new jobs while American controlled companies created only 1,500 new jobs on a net basis. Yet in the same period the share of total corporate profits by American companies rose from 31 per cent of the total to 43 per cent of
January 19, 1988

the total. American controlled companies saw their profits double to $17 billion. It is particularly telling to note that for every $1 billion in profits, Canadian companies created 5,700 jobs. For every $1 billion in profits, American controlled companies created 17 jobs and no more.
The Minister has no understanding about the degree to which Canada is being shortchanged by foreign investment and foreign-controlled companies in this country. There has been a buying spree by American companies in Canada, which has been documented by Investment Canada and which affected firms with 100,000 employees in 1986-87. There is no indication that we will be able to have any condition at all to make sure those companies act on behalf of Canadians, to protect Canadian jobs, do research and development here in Canada, buy from Canadian sources, and develop unique Canadian inventions in Canada. None of that will be required. Furthermore, we have the evidence that these companies are not creating jobs.
I stated during Question Period on October 7 that the Government was giving up our right to protect Canadian jobs. I cited the situation at Firestone.
The Minister said my allegations were absolutely false and without foundation and did not deserve a further answer. Fortunatel. the rules of the House allow me to seek a further answer and I call on the Minister to support her spurious allegations which are totally in contradiction with the facts. The facts are that Canadian companies have been creating the jobs in Canada in the last seven or eight years and American-controlled companies are taking the profits but not creating the jobs. Yet the Government wants Canada to enter into a free trade agreement that will abandon any means by which our Government and Canadians asking the Government to act for them can ensure that there is a requirement of good corporate performance and citizenship by American companies which are operating and moving into Canada. I call on the Minister or her Parliamentary Secretary to refute my case.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Council of Canadians obtained figures from Statistics Canada on employment levels, indicating a difference between the number of jobs created by Canadian firms and firms under foreign control between 1978 and 1985.
Adjournment Debate
We can draw three conclusions from this information. First, there is a very close correlation between employment levels and business size. Everybody knows that small businesses are responsible for most of the increase in employment levels in Canada.
Second, over the period in question employment dropped in manufacturing and increased in the service sector, whether firms were Canadian or foreign-owned.
Third and last, the information does not indicate that foreign investment is harmful to the economy or that foreign-controlled companies are less likely to create jobs.
That sounds too good to be true!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I suggest the Hon. Member take a deep breath to get some oxygen to his brain.
A careful analysis of the Statistics Canada figures would also have considered the investment policy of the Government at the time. Remember, we are talking about the period between 1978 and 1985. During that time, foreign investment in Canada was discouraged with policies like the National Energy Program and the Foreign Investment Review Act. In fact, between 1978 and 1985, the number of foreign-controlled firms dropped from 3,838 to 3,179. Since there were fewer large firms that were foreign-controlled, it is not surprising that large companies contributed less to raising employment levels then small companies.
New foreign investment will be crucial to economic growth, innovation and trade within a free-trade zone. Consequently, within the framework of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, both countries have developed a set of principles that will help increase transborder investment flow. Canada has retained the right to monitor significant takeovers by U.S. investors. The minimum review level for direct takeovers will be raised to $150 million in four years, in other words by 1992. By that time, about two-thirds of all non-financial assets in Canada will still be subject to review.
Mr. Speaker, monitoring of indirect takeovers, involving the transfer of control of a foreign-controlled business to another business will be gradually phased out over the same period.
